0.title: In the Beginning: The Book of Origins
0.overview:
Genesis is the book of beginnings — and every beginning in the Bible finds its root here. The creation of the cosmos, the dignity of humanity as image-bearers of God, the catastrophe of the fall, the first promise of redemption, the flood and new creation, the scattering of nations, and then the extraordinary narrowing of God's redemptive focus onto one man, one family, one people through whom all the families of the earth will be blessed (12:3). To read Genesis is to stand at the headwaters of everything that follows in Scripture.

The book divides naturally into two great movements. The primeval history (chapters 1–11) moves from creation to catastrophe to new beginning — from the garden of Eden to the tower of Babel — tracing the spread of sin and the persistence of grace. The patriarchal history (chapters 12–50) follows Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph, tracing the covenant God makes and keeps across four generations in spite of every human failure. Throughout both movements, one thread holds everything together: the seed of the woman (3:15), the promise that will not be extinguished, the line that leads through flood and famine and fratricide and exile to the One who crushes the serpent's head.

Genesis is also the fountainhead of the Bible's great typological stream. Adam is the type of the One to come (Romans 5:14) — and where Adam fails, Christ succeeds. The sacrifice of Isaac on Moriah (chapter 22) is the most luminous prefiguration of Calvary in the Old Testament: a father, a son, a mountain, a substitute, and the word of the LORD: "The LORD will provide." Joseph — rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, condemned unjustly, exalted to the right hand of power, and the savior of the very brothers who betrayed him — is the most sustained type of Christ in Genesis, and one of the most beautiful in all of Scripture.

The theological lens throughout this commentary is Reformed and christological, drawing especially on Timothy Keller's Genesis sermon series at Redeemer Presbyterian Church, John Calvin's Commentary on Genesis, Derek Kidner's Genesis (Tyndale Old Testament Commentaries), Bruce Waltke's Genesis: A Commentary, and Gordon Wenham's Genesis (Word Biblical Commentary). The governing conviction is that Genesis is not a problem to be defended but a gift to be received — and that every page, rightly read, leads to Jesus Christ, in whom all the promises of God find their Yes and Amen (2 Corinthians 1:20).

1.title: In the Beginning, God
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth. <sup>2</sup>The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters. <sup>3</sup>And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. <sup>26</sup>Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth." <sup>27</sup>So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them. <sup>28</sup>And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it." <sup>31</sup>And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.
1.overview:
The first verse of Genesis is the most momentous sentence ever written: "In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth." Before the cosmos, before time, before anything — there was God. Creation is not God (pantheism), and matter is not evil (dualism) — it is the good gift of a God who exists in glorious self-sufficiency and chooses to bring another into existence out of pure generosity.

The sovereign creative word — "and God said" — echoes ten times through the chapter, each time calling something new into existence. The same Word that spoke at creation became flesh in Jesus Christ (John 1:1–3; Col. 1:16). Creation is a trinitarian act: the Father creates, the Spirit hovers, the Son is the Word through whom all things are made.

The climax is the creation of humanity in the image of God (imago Dei, vv.26–27). Unlike every other element of creation, humanity is made not by divine command but by divine deliberation — "Let us make" — and is stamped with the divine likeness. This image is not a faculty but a relational and vocational reality: humanity is made to represent God in the world and rule the creation as vice-regents under his lordship. The chapter closes with the Creator's own verdict: "it was very good."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Creation Days One through Three
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis opens not with argument but with proclamation: God created. The majestic, measured cadence of the creation account — God speaks, it is so, God sees that it is good, evening and morning — establishes the sovereignty, goodness, and rationality of the Creator before any human being appears. Days one through three bring order out of formlessness: light separated from darkness, waters above from waters below, dry land distinguished from sea, and the earth clothed with vegetation.
verseByVerse.theology: Creation ex nihilo — from nothing — is the foundational theological claim of verse 1. God does not shape pre-existing matter; he speaks reality into existence. The Spirit hovering over the waters anticipates the new creation theology of the New Testament (2 Cor. 5:17; John 1:1–3). The repeated 'it was good' is a moral and aesthetic verdict, not merely utilitarian: the created order reflects the character of its Creator. Wenham notes the symmetrical structure of days 1–6 (days 1–3 form the domains; days 4–6 fill them) reveals intentional, literary artistry that signals theological purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Waltke observes that the creation account is simultaneously polemical — countering ancient Near Eastern cosmogonies where chaos gods battle — and doxological, inviting worship of the Creator. Kidner notes that 'formless and void' (tohu wabohu) is the antithesis of everything God will accomplish: purposeful order from purposeless chaos. This is the pattern of all God's redemptive work — creating order, beauty, and life where there was only darkness and void.

verseByVerse.quote: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Ten Hebrew words that changed everything. Before time, before space, before matter — God. The verb bara (created) is used in Scripture only with God as subject; it denotes a category of action available to no creature. "The heavens and the earth" is a Hebrew merism for the totality of all that exists. This verse is not merely a historical claim but a theological foundation: the universe is not self-existent, not eternal, not divine — it is the product of a personal God who acted freely and purposefully. Waltke writes that this single sentence dismantles every form of materialism, pantheism, and dualism simultaneously. Everything that follows in Scripture is commentary on this fact.

verseByVerse.quote: The earth was without form and void, and darkness was over the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters.
verseByVerse.commentary: The initial state of creation is chaotic, unordered, dark — not because God failed but because the work of ordering and filling is about to begin. "Formless and void" (tohu wabohu) describes an earth not yet shaped for habitation. The darkness is not evil here but the raw material of creation, soon to yield to light. The Spirit of God hovering over the waters — the Hebrew word for hovering is used of an eagle over its young (Deut. 32:11) — signals divine presence, care, and imminent action. Wenham notes this is the first Trinitarian hint in Scripture: God (v.1), Spirit (v.2), and Word (v.3) are all present at creation's beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. And God saw that the light was good. And God separated the light from the darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary: Creation proceeds by divine speech — not struggle, not labor, not negotiation. God speaks and reality obeys. This is the power of the word of God that will recur throughout Scripture: the spoken word that creates, heals, raises the dead, and finally is enfleshed in the Son (John 1:1–3). The light created here precedes the sun (created day four), which the ancient world worshiped. Kidner notes that by creating light independently of the sun, the text demythologizes the celestial bodies — they are creatures, not gods. God's verdict — "it was good" — is the first moral evaluation in Scripture: the Creator's work reflects his own goodness.

verseByVerse.quote: God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, the first day.
verseByVerse.commentary: God names what he creates, exercising sovereign authority over his creation — naming in the ancient world was an act of lordship and definition. The pattern "evening and morning, the N day" will structure the entire creation account. The ordering of evening before morning reflects Hebrew reckoning (the day beginning at sunset) but also theological truth: out of darkness, light comes; out of death, life. This pattern culminates in the resurrection, where the darkest evening gives way to the brightest morning. Calvin writes that the regularity of days in creation established the order by which God would govern his creation throughout history.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be an expanse in the midst of the waters, and let it separate the waters from the waters." And God made the expanse and separated the waters that were under the expanse from the waters that were above the expanse. And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second day brings vertical ordering: the watery chaos is divided into waters above and below the expanse (the sky/atmosphere). Ancient cosmology conceived of water above the sky as the source of rain; God separates and governs these waters, establishing the ordered system that sustains life. "And it was so" — the phrase of divine authority — recurs like a liturgical refrain. God does not propose; he decrees. Waltke notes that the creation of the expanse establishes the inhabitable space between waters, a kind of cosmic room being prepared for the life and human community that will come.

verseByVerse.quote: And God called the expanse Heaven. And there was evening and there was morning, the second day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The expanse is named Heaven — the sky, the firmament, the dome of creation. Again naming signals sovereignty: God defines and governs the domains he creates. Uniquely, no "it was good" appears after day two, leading commentators to various explanations. Wenham suggests the absence is intentional — day two's work is incomplete until day five fills the expanse with birds. The creation account is architecturally structured so that days 1–3 create domains and days 4–6 fill them; day two's domain (sky) awaits its filling on day five. The pattern teaches that God's purposes unfold in sequence, each stage preparing for the next.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters under the heavens be gathered together into one place, and let the dry land appear." And it was so. God called the dry land Earth, and the waters that were gathered together he called Seas. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary: Day three begins with the separation of land from sea — the earth emerging from the waters as a habitable domain. The language echoes Israel's experience at the Red Sea (Exod. 14:21–22) and anticipates the new creation (Rev. 21:1). God names both the dry land and the seas, asserting authority over both. Kidner notes that the sea, which in ancient Near Eastern mythology represented chaos and threat, is here simply a creature doing what God commanded — gathered, named, bounded. The God of Genesis rules chaos; he does not fight it. "It was good" — the land and sea are evaluated as fitting for life, for the vegetation about to appear.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth sprout vegetation, plants yielding seed, and fruit trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind, on the earth." And it was so. The earth brought forth vegetation, plants yielding seed according to their own kinds, and trees bearing fruit in which is their seed, each according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary: The earth itself is commanded to produce vegetation — the land becomes a participant in creation, responsive to God's word. "Each according to its kind" appears repeatedly in the creation account, establishing the ordered diversity of life: God is not a chaotic creator but one who gives each living thing its own identity and reproductive pattern. The seed-bearing principle ensures continuity and abundance — each plant carries within it the capacity for multiplication. Wenham observes that vegetation precedes animals and humans, establishing the food supply before the consumers. The provision is built into the structure of creation itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was evening and there was morning, the third day.
verseByVerse.commentary: Day three is the most productive of the first three days: both the separation of land from sea (vv.9–10) and the creation of vegetation (vv.11–12) occur on this day, earning two "it was good" evaluations. This double verdict on day three corresponds to day six's double work of land animals and humanity. The structure is not arbitrary but reflects careful literary and theological artistry. The creation narrative is composed to be read, contemplated, and recited — Calvin notes that Moses wrote for the people of God to understand, not for scientific specialists, presenting the grandeur of creation in terms accessible to all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–31 — Creation Days Four through Six: Lights, Living Creatures, and the Image of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second triad of creation fills the domains established in days one through three. The lights fill the sky and govern time; sea creatures and birds fill the waters and expanse; land animals and finally humanity fill the earth. The account builds to its climax in the creation of the human being in the image of God — male and female — entrusted with dominion over the whole creation. God's final verdict on the completed creation is not merely 'good' but 'very good.'
verseByVerse.theology: The image of God (imago Dei) in verse 26–27 is the theological summit of Genesis 1. Human beings are not the product of chance or the plaything of capricious deities but the intentional creation of God, bearing his image and entrusted with his delegated authority over creation. The image involves rationality, morality, relationality, and the capacity for dominion — reflecting God's own character as one who orders, names, evaluates, and rules. The creation of male and female together as image-bearers establishes the equality of the sexes in dignity before any distinction in role is introduced.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller's 'The Reason for God' and his Genesis sermons are essential here: he argues that Genesis 1 presents the cosmos as a temple — structured, ordered, God-filled — with humanity as the priests who serve within it. Waltke notes that the creation mandate (be fruitful, multiply, fill, subdue, have dominion) is the first word God speaks to humans, defining their purpose before any prohibition appears. Dominion is stewardship, not exploitation: humans rule on God's behalf, accountable to the Creator whose image they bear.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens to separate the day from the night. And let them be for signs and for seasons, and for days and years, and let them be lights in the expanse of the heavens to give light upon the earth." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary: The lights are created on day four to govern time — separating day from night and marking seasons, days, and years. Their function is practical (light for life) and temporal (ordering human existence within time). "Signs and seasons" includes the sacred calendar — the feasts and appointed times of Israel will be tied to the movements of sun and moon. Critically, the sun and moon are not named; in ancient Near Eastern texts their names were names of deities. By withholding their names, Genesis demythologizes the celestial bodies: they are lights, creatures, servants of God's ordering purposes, not objects of worship. Wenham calls this the most radical anti-idolatry statement in the ancient world.

verseByVerse.quote: And God made the two great lights—the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night—and the stars. And God set them in the expanse of the heavens to give light on the earth,
verseByVerse.commentary: "The two great lights" — not sun and moon by name, a deliberate refusal to use the names of pagan deities. And the stars — added almost parenthetically, as if the objects of Babylonian astronomical religion are a footnote in God's creation agenda. God made them; God set them in place; they serve his purposes. The verb "to rule" (memsheleth) is royal language — the lights govern their domains under God's higher authority. Calvin notes that the apparent smallness of the stars is addressed: they appear tiny but God has set each in its place for a purpose, and faith reads the heavens not as divine powers but as the handiwork of the Creator.

verseByVerse.quote: to rule over the day and over the night, and to separate the light from the darkness. And God saw that it was good. And there was evening and there was morning, the fourth day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The function of the lights — to rule and to separate — echoes the ordering work of day one (separating light from darkness). Day four fills day one's domain; the parallel structure is intentional. "God saw that it was good" — the created order, including the vast and mysterious cosmos, bears the character of its Maker. The regularity of days and seasons that the lights govern is not merely practical but covenantal: God will later promise Noah that "seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, shall not cease" (8:22). The lights are part of God's covenant faithfulness embedded in creation itself.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the waters swarm with swarms of living creatures, and let birds fly above the earth across the expanse of the heavens." So God created the great sea creatures and every living creature that moves, with which the waters swarm, according to their kinds, and every winged bird according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary: Day five fills the domains of day two — the sea and sky. The Hebrew tanninim ("great sea creatures") are elsewhere the dragons or monsters of chaos in ancient Near Eastern mythology; here they are simply creatures God made, without drama or combat. God speaks and sea monsters exist — as his servants, not as his rivals. "Each according to its kind" again emphasizes the orderly diversity of creation. Wenham notes that the sheer abundance of sea life — "swarms" — reflects God's delight in profusion and variety. The God of creation is lavish, not minimal; he fills his creation with more life than seems necessary, reflecting his own inexhaustible generosity.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them, saying, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the waters in the seas, and let birds multiply on the earth." And there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first blessing in Scripture is spoken over living creatures — God's benediction establishes the reproductive principle as a gift, not merely a biological fact. "Be fruitful and multiply and fill" is the same language later spoken to humanity (v.28) and to Noah (9:1), suggesting that the blessing of abundance is a fundamental expression of God's goodness toward his creatures. Waltke observes that the blessing makes the creatures participants in the ongoing work of creation — they carry forward the filling of the earth by divine commission. This is what it means for creatures to serve God: not mere mechanical function but blessed, purposeful activity aligned with the Creator's intentions.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Let the earth bring forth living creatures according to their kinds—livestock and creeping things and beasts of the earth according to their kinds." And it was so. And God made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds and the livestock according to their kinds, and everything that creeps on the ground according to its kind. And God saw that it was good.
verseByVerse.commentary: Day six begins with land animals, filling the domain of day three. Three categories — livestock, creeping things, wild beasts — represent the comprehensive range of land life. The earth again participates in production: "let the earth bring forth." The creation responds to God's word by generating life from its own materials. This anticipates the creation of Adam from the dust of the ground (2:7) — humanity shares its material origin with the other creatures, which both connects us to creation and sets up the contrast of the divine image. God sees that it is good — but the day is not yet complete.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God said, "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness. And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth." So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The creation of humanity is marked by four unique features: the deliberative "let us make" (suggesting inner-Trinitarian counsel), the image and likeness language, the grant of dominion, and the immediate affirmation of male and female. "Image" (tselem) was used of statues representing a king in his territory; to be God's image is to represent God's rule in the creation. This is not primarily about intellect or moral capacity (though these are included) but about function: humans are placed in creation as God's viceroys. The threefold repetition of "image" in v.27 underscores its importance. Male and female together bear the image — neither alone exhausts it. Keller writes that human dignity is not earned but given, not achieved but bestowed.

verseByVerse.quote: And God blessed them. And God said to them, "Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over every living thing that moves on the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary: The creation mandate is God's first word to humanity: bless, multiply, fill, subdue, have dominion. This is not the command to exploit but to steward — to exercise God's own authority on God's behalf. "Subdue" (kabash) involves bringing order and fruitfulness to the earth through human work and culture; "have dominion" (radah) is royal authority modeled on God's own rule. Together they define what it means to be human: creature, image-bearer, regent, and worker. Waltke notes that the cultural mandate — making civilizations, cultivating creation, governing its creatures — is grounded in the character of God himself, who created by ordering, naming, evaluating, and ruling.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said, "Behold, I have given you every plant yielding seed that is on the face of all the earth, and every tree with seed in its fruit. You shall have them for food. And to every beast of the earth and to every bird of the heavens and to everything that creeps on the earth, everything that has the breath of life, I have given every green plant for food." And it was so.
verseByVerse.commentary: Before any prohibition, God speaks provision: the entire plant kingdom is given as food. This lavish grant establishes the Creator's generosity as the baseline of human experience — we live in a world of abundant gift before we encounter any restriction. The vegetarian diet for both humans and animals in the original creation suggests a peaceable relationship between creatures; the permission to eat meat comes only after the flood (9:3). Kidner observes that this original harmony between humans and creation will be fractured by sin but restored in the new creation (Isa. 65:25), making the current state of the world a parenthesis between two versions of shalom.

verseByVerse.quote: And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good. And there was evening and there was morning, the sixth day.
verseByVerse.commentary: The climactic verdict over the completed creation is not merely "good" but "very good" — the superlative reserved for day six when the creation reaches its God-intended fullness with the image-bearer present. The creation is good not because God approved of what happened to exist accidentally but because it perfectly reflects his creative intentions. Evil, suffering, and death are not original features of the universe but intrusions — the story of redemption is the story of God restoring what sin corrupted. Calvin writes that this verse is the basis for a robustly positive Christian engagement with the material world: it is God's good creation, the theater of his glory, and worth working to restore and cultivate.

1.theology:
The Trinity in Creation. Genesis 1 contains seeds the New Testament flowers. The Spirit hovers (v.2); God speaks his Word (v.3); the Father creates (v.1). John 1:1–3 identifies the creative Word with the eternal Son: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made." Colossians 1:16 and Hebrews 1:2 confirm: the universe was made through and for Christ. Creation is a trinitarian act.

The Image of God and Human Dignity. The imago Dei (vv.26–27) is the theological foundation of every claim about human dignity — not achievement, intelligence, beauty, or utility, but the image of God stamped on every human being from conception. This is why the taking of human life is an assault on God himself (Gen. 9:6). In an age of competing accounts of human value, Genesis 1:27 remains the most radical claim ever made: every person bears the image of the Creator of the cosmos.
1.examples:
Then: Israel's neighbors had elaborate creation myths — the Babylonian Enuma Elish featured warring gods and humanity created as divine slave labor. Genesis 1 is a quiet, majestic polemic: one God, sovereign speech, ordered goodness, humanity as image-bearers rather than slaves. The chapter was simultaneously theological and political — a declaration that Israel's God alone is Creator and Lord.

Now: Contemporary cosmology traces the universe to a beginning (the Big Bang), confirming what Genesis asserted millennia ago. But science cannot tell us whether the beginning had a Beholder. Genesis answers with the confidence of revelation. And the imago Dei cuts against every modern reductionism — the person reduced to their productivity, genome, or social utility has had their image-bearing dignity denied. The church holds the most radical account of human worth available in the contemporary marketplace of ideas.

2.title: The LORD God Formed the Man
2.text: <sup>7</sup>Then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature. <sup>8</sup>And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed. <sup>15</sup>The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it. <sup>16</sup>And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, <sup>17</sup>but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die." <sup>18</sup>Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him." <sup>24</sup>Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh. <sup>25</sup>And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
2.overview:
Where Genesis 1 surveys creation from the cosmic perspective, Genesis 2 zooms in — camera descending from the heavens to settle on a garden, a man formed from dust, the breath of God filling his lungs. The change of divine name is significant: chapter 1 uses Elohim (God, the transcendent Creator); chapter 2 introduces YHWH Elohim (the LORD God), the covenant name that will define all of Israel's subsequent relationship with this God. The Creator is not merely a force but a Person who walks in gardens and calls for conversation.

The garden of Eden is not merely a pleasant park but a sacred space — a temple-garden where God dwells with humanity. The man's vocation to "work it and keep it" (v.15) uses the same Hebrew verbs (abad and shamar) used later for priestly service in the tabernacle (Num. 3:7–8). Adam is simultaneously a gardener and a priest — his work is worship and his worship is work.

The creation of woman is the chapter's climax. "It is not good that the man should be alone" (v.18) — the first "not good" in Genesis — reveals that even paradise without community is incomplete. Marriage is the first human institution, established before the fall. Paul calls it a "profound mystery" that images Christ's union with the church (Eph. 5:31–32) — and Jesus upholds its creational authority when asked about divorce (Matt. 19:4–6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Seventh Day and the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creation account concludes with the Sabbath rest of God — the first holy time in Scripture — and then zooms in to tell the story of human origins with vivid particularity. Chapter 2 is not a contradiction of chapter 1 but a complementary close-up: where chapter 1 gives the cosmic panorama, chapter 2 gives the intimate portrait of the man formed from dust and the woman formed from his side, placed in a garden designed for abundance and communion with God.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath rest of God (vv.1–3) is the theological and temporal crown of creation: God rests not from exhaustion but in sovereign completion, blessing the seventh day as a pattern for human life and worship. The garden of Eden is not merely paradise but a sanctuary — the place where God walks with his image-bearers in unhindered communion. The two trees at the center — life and the knowledge of good and evil — represent the two dimensions of the human condition: dependence on God for life, and the question of moral allegiance. The prohibition of the tree of knowledge is not arbitrary but constitutive of the creature-Creator relationship.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 2: the garden is a temple, Eden is the innermost sanctuary, and Adam is the priest-king who serves within it. Wenham notes that the terms used for Adam's work in the garden — 'to work' (abad) and 'to keep' (shamar) — are the same terms used for priestly service in the tabernacle (Num. 3:7–8; 8:26). Human vocation begins as priestly: maintaining and guarding the sacred space of God's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God finished his work that he had done, and he rested on the seventh day from all his work that he had done.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Finished" — the creation is complete, whole, lacking nothing. The word translated "host" (tsaba) refers to the vast armies of creatures filling sky and earth; the entire company of creation is in place. God's rest on the seventh day is not divine fatigue but divine completion — the act of a sovereign who surveys his accomplished work and dwells in its fullness. The Sabbath rest is the eschatological goal of creation: Hebrews 3–4 teaches that believers are invited into this divine rest, which the original Sabbath anticipates. Waltke notes that God's rest is also God's enthronement — the creator-king taking his throne in the creation he has completed.

verseByVerse.quote: So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation.
verseByVerse.commentary: The seventh day receives two distinctions given to nothing else in chapter 1: blessing and holiness. Holy (qadosh) means set apart, distinguished, different in character. Time itself is consecrated — before any place or person is called holy, a day is. The Sabbath principle embedded in creation means that rest and worship are not afterthoughts to human productivity but the rhythmic heart of God's design for human life. Calvin writes that God blessed the Sabbath for human benefit: the day of rest is given not because God needed it but because humanity would. The fourth commandment (Exod. 20:8–11) grounds the Sabbath explicitly in the creation pattern of these verses.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens. When no bush of the field was yet in the land and no small plant of the field had yet sprung up—for the LORD God had not yet caused it to rain on the land, and there was no man to work the ground,
verseByVerse.commentary: "These are the generations" — a formula that introduces a new section in Genesis (toledoth), here marking the transition from cosmic creation to human history. Significantly, the divine name shifts from Elohim (God as cosmic Creator) to YHWH Elohim (the LORD God) — adding the covenant name to the creative one. This is the first use of YHWH in Scripture, the personal name of Israel's God who revealed himself to Moses (Exod. 3:14). Wenham notes that the pre-creation condition described (no rain, no man to work) establishes that creation without human cultivation is incomplete — humanity's vocation of working the ground is part of the design from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: and a mist was going up from the land and was watering the whole face of the ground— then the LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature.
verseByVerse.commentary: The formation of Adam combines dust and divine breath — material and immaterial, creature and creation, earth and heaven. "Formed" (yatsar) is the potter's word, suggesting careful, personal craftsmanship. The dust links humanity to the earth — we share our matter with the ground and will return to it (3:19). The breath of life (nishmat hayyim) distinguishes humanity from all other creatures: God does not breathe into the animals but does breathe into Adam, establishing an intimacy of origin unique to the image-bearer. Kidner notes that the result — a "living creature" (nephesh hayyah) — uses the same term applied to animals (1:24), but what makes Adam different is the divine breath that animates the dust. We are more than animals because we are God-breathed.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God planted a garden in Eden, in the east, and there he put the man whom he had formed. And out of the ground the LORD God made to spring up every tree that is pleasant to the sight and good for food. The tree of life was in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
verseByVerse.commentary: God himself plants the garden — an act of personal provision for the creature he has just formed. Eden means "delight" or "pleasure"; the garden is a place designed for human flourishing. The trees are both beautiful and nourishing — God's provision satisfies the aesthetic as well as the physical. At the center stand two trees with cosmic significance: the tree of life (access to immortality) and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (the question of moral sovereignty). Waltke notes that their central placement means human life is organized around these two realities: dependence on God for life, and the question of who determines right and wrong — God or the creature.

verseByVerse.quote: A river flowed out of Eden to water the garden, and there it divided and became four rivers. The name of the first is the Pishon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.
verseByVerse.commentary: The geography of Eden connects the garden to the known world, grounding the narrative in real history rather than mythology. Four rivers flowing from Eden suggest that the garden is the source of life and blessing for the entire earth — the center from which goodness flows outward. The mention of gold and precious stones signals that Eden is a place of cosmic value, not merely biological abundance. Keller notes that the garden-temple imagery is reinforced by these details: the tabernacle and later the temple were adorned with gold and precious stones (Exod. 25:7; 1 Kings 6–7), deliberately echoing Eden's original splendor. Sacred space and created abundance belong together in God's design.

verseByVerse.quote: And the gold of that land is good; bdellium and onyx stone are there. The name of the second river is the Gihon. It is the one that flowed around the whole land of Cush.
verseByVerse.commentary: The precious materials of Havilah — gold, bdellium (a fragrant resin), and onyx — will reappear in the construction of the tabernacle and priestly garments (Exod. 25:7; 28:9–12), connecting Israel's worship to the original Edenic sanctuary. The Gihon river, associated with Cush (Ethiopia/Sudan), traces the garden's blessings southward. The author's specificity — naming rivers and lands — is deliberate; Eden is not a dreamscape but a real place whose glory was historically present and historically lost. The loss of Eden is not mythological but theological: something real was forfeited at the fall, and something real will be restored in the new Jerusalem (Rev. 22:1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: The name of the third river is the Tigris, which flows east of Assyria. And the fourth river is the Euphrates.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Tigris and Euphrates are the great rivers of Mesopotamia — known geography to ancient readers. Their inclusion alongside the less-known Pishon and Gihon anchors Eden in a real region of the ancient Near East, likely in or near Mesopotamia. This geographical specificity means the creation account cannot be safely spiritualized into timeless myth; it makes historical claims about a real garden, real rivers, and real events. Wenham notes that scholars debate the precise location, but the theological point is clear: the garden is the original homeland of humanity, the place of perfect communion with God that sin removed and that redemption restores.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Work" (abad) and "keep" (shamar) — two Hebrew words that define Adam's vocation. Abad means to serve, to cultivate, to till; shamar means to guard, to watch over, to preserve. Together they describe a stewardship that is both active (cultivating, developing) and protective (guarding against harm). These are also the priestly terms for tabernacle service — Adam is both gardener and priest, both worker and warden. Waltke writes that human work is not a consequence of the fall but part of the original design: we were made to be creative stewards, and the dignity of labor is grounded in God's own creative work and the task he assigned his image-bearers from the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, "You may surely eat of every tree of the garden, but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die."
verseByVerse.commentary: God's first words to Adam in chapter 2 are a permission (eat freely of every tree) and a prohibition (not this one tree). The permission vastly outnumbers the prohibition — the garden is a place of abundance and freedom, not restriction. The prohibition is not arbitrary but constitutive of the creature-Creator relationship: "the knowledge of good and evil" means the autonomous determination of moral categories — arrogating to oneself the right to define right and wrong independently of God. Kidner notes that the issue is not information (Adam already knows much) but authority: who has the right to set the moral order? The warning — "you shall surely die" — establishes death as the consequence of moral rebellion, not as a natural biological endpoint. Death entered through sin (Rom. 5:12).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — The Creation of Woman and the First Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The creation of Eve completes the image of God in humanity and establishes marriage as the foundational human institution. God's declaration that "it is not good" for man to be alone is the first 'not good' in Scripture — interrupting the rhythm of 'it was good' from chapter 1 to underscore that human beings are inherently relational. The woman is not an afterthought but the completion of what the man could not be alone.
verseByVerse.theology: The creation of woman from Adam's side establishes both her equality (same flesh, same nature, image-bearer equally) and her distinctiveness (formed differently, described as helper and complement). The marriage covenant — leaving, cleaving, becoming one flesh — is the human institution that most directly reflects the divine image's relational nature. Jesus will later appeal to this text (Matt. 19:4–6) as the permanent basis of marriage, and Paul will read it as a type of Christ and the church (Eph. 5:31–32).
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that 'helper' (ezer) is not a term of subordination — it is used of God himself as Israel's helper (Ps. 121:2). The woman is a helper in the sense of completing what is lacking — providing what the man cannot provide for himself. Keller observes that the nakedness without shame (v.25) describes a state of perfect transparency and trust between the man and woman, which sin will shatter and redemption will ultimately restore.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first "not good" in Scripture — and it appears before the fall. Aloneness, not sin, is the first thing God declares insufficient. This is a profound statement about human nature: we are made for relationship, for community, for the other. "Helper fit for him" (ezer kenegdo) means a helper corresponding to him — a complementary counterpart, not a subordinate copy. Waltke notes that kenegdo literally means "as in front of him" — someone who faces him, who is his equal and his opposite, who completes what is lacking. The creation of woman is not a correction of creation but the completion of it. The image of God, established in Genesis 1:27 as male and female together, requires both to be present.

verseByVerse.quote: Now out of the ground the LORD God had formed every beast of the field and every bird of the heavens and brought them to the man to see what he would call them. And whatever the man called every living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all livestock and to the birds of the heavens and to every beast of the field. But for Adam there was not found a helper fit for him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The naming of the animals is both a royal act (exercising dominion, as in chapter 1) and a revelatory process: Adam surveys all living creatures and discovers that none is a fitting companion. The parade of animals is not a failed attempt at finding a match but the necessary demonstration that the woman must come from a different source — not from the ground like the animals but from the man himself. God "watches" Adam name the animals — "to see what he would call them" — suggesting genuine human creativity in partnership with divine initiative. Kidner notes that the naming of animals is the first human act in Scripture and establishes the pattern: human culture, including language itself, is a fulfillment of the creation mandate.

verseByVerse.quote: So the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon the man, and while he slept took one of his ribs and closed up its place with flesh. And the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man he made into a woman and brought her to the man.
verseByVerse.commentary: The deep sleep (tardemah) is elsewhere in Scripture a state of divine action upon a person (15:12; 1 Sam. 26:12) — Adam is not a passive observer but a recipient of grace while unconscious. The rib from Adam's side has generated rich reflection: Wenham notes the rib is not the head (suggesting dominion) or the foot (suggesting subjection) but the side, suggesting equality and partnership. Augustine wrote that woman was taken not from Adam's head to be above him, nor from his feet to be below him, but from his side to stand alongside him. The woman is brought to the man — God acts as the father who presents the bride to the bridegroom, establishing marriage as a covenantal institution with divine foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the man said, "This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary: The first human words in Scripture are a poem — a joyful, astonished recognition of the woman as the one who corresponds to the man perfectly. "This at last" — the Hebrew suggests relief and delight after the long parade of animals: here is what I was looking for. "Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" is a covenant formula (cf. 29:14; 2 Sam. 5:1) indicating the deepest possible identification — she is not other but self extended. The man names the woman (ishah) from himself (ish) — a recognition that their identities are inseparable. This naming differs from the naming of animals; it is not lordship over another creature but recognition of shared nature and covenantal bond.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrator's comment — "therefore" — draws out the normative principle from the creation narrative: marriage involves leaving (primary loyalty shifts from family of origin), cleaving (covenant commitment, the word suggests glue or welding), and becoming one flesh (comprehensive union — physical, emotional, covenantal). The order is significant: leaving precedes cleaving, which precedes one-flesh union. Marriage is not merely a social arrangement or a legal contract but the re-union of what was originally one — a return to the wholeness that existed before woman was formed from man. Jesus will cite this verse as the permanent, creation-order foundation of marriage (Matt. 19:5), and Paul reads it as a type of Christ's union with the church (Eph. 5:31–32).

verseByVerse.quote: And the man and his wife were both naked and were not ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final verse of chapter 2 describes the condition of created humanity before the fall: naked and unashamed. Nakedness without shame is not merely physical exposure but total transparency — no hiding, no pretense, no self-protection, no fear of the other's judgment. It describes a relationship of perfect trust and openness between the man and the woman, and implicitly between both of them and God. Wenham notes that the shame introduced by the fall (3:7, 10) is the direct inverse of this verse: sin produces the need to cover and hide what was once openly shared. The restoration of this shameless transparency — not just physical but spiritual — is part of what the gospel promises: acceptance, justification, and the removal of the condemning gaze of God and self.

2.theology:
The Garden as Temple. Eden is the original sacred space — the place where heaven and earth overlap, where God walks with humanity. The imagery recurs in the tabernacle (gold, cherubim, guarded entrance) and temple. Revelation 21–22 closes the canon with the new Jerusalem as a garden-city in which the temple is the Lord God himself: God and humanity dwelling together without barrier, the original vision of Eden fully restored and surpassed.

The Second Adam. Paul's argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 turns on the contrast between Adam and Christ. Adam, formed from dust, given every permission, faced one prohibition, failed, and brought death to all. Christ, the eternal Son who took on flesh, faced every temptation the first Adam faced, obeyed perfectly, and brought life to all in him. The garden of Gethsemane is the counter-garden of Eden: where Adam chose his will over God's, Christ prayed "not my will, but yours be done."
2.examples:
Then: The garden-temple imagery was immediately legible to an Israelite audience familiar with the tabernacle. The cherubim guarding Eden's entrance (3:24) matched the cherubim woven into the tabernacle veil. The gold and onyx of Eden (2:11–12) matched the temple's materials. The man's priestly vocation prepared Israel to understand the priesthood as a restoration project — attempting to restore, through ritual, the access to God's presence lost at the fall.

Now: The theology of work in Genesis 2 is urgently needed in a culture that either deifies career (finding identity in productivity) or denigrates it (work as mere necessity). Genesis 2 says: work is a gift before it is a burden, a vocation before it is a job. And the chapter's account of gender and marriage — the complementarity of male and female, the one-flesh covenant, the goodness of embodiment — flows from creation design, not cultural construction. To recover a theology of Genesis 2 is to recover a theology of the human person.

3.title: The Fall
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?" <sup>4</sup>But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. <sup>5</sup>For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil." <sup>6</sup>So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate. <sup>7</sup>Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. <sup>15</sup>"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel." <sup>21</sup>And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is the hinge of all human history — the chapter that makes every other chapter in the Bible necessary. Without the fall, there is no need for a flood, a covenant, a law, a temple, a sacrifice, a prophet, a Messiah, a cross, or a resurrection. Every subsequent movement of Scripture is a movement of redemption, and redemption only makes sense in light of what is lost here.

The serpent's strategy is a masterpiece of misdirection. He begins not with a command but with a question: "Did God actually say?" — casting doubt on the divine word, then on the divine motive. The lie is plausible. "You will be like God" — and they already were, made in his image. The serpent offers a counterfeit of what they already possess. This is the anatomy of every temptation: the distortion of a good thing into a god-thing.

But before any judgment is announced, God speaks the first gospel — the protevangelium of verse 15: the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head. And before expelling them from the garden, God clothes them with skins — the first sacrifice, the first covering of shame by divine grace. The gospel is embedded in the fall itself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Temptation and the Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 3 is the hinge of all Scripture — the pivot between creation's goodness and the fallen world we inhabit. The serpent's strategy is subtle: not a frontal assault on God's existence but a quiet questioning of his goodness. Eve is drawn into dialogue, then doubt, then desire, then action. Adam stands passively by and eats. In a moment, the entire fabric of human life with God is torn. The nakedness and hiding that follow are the symptoms of a rupture that touches every dimension of existence.
verseByVerse.theology: The fall narrative reveals the anatomy of sin: the serpent distorts God's word ('Did God actually say?'), denies God's judgment ('You will not surely die'), and substitutes a counterfeit promise ('You will be like God'). Eve evaluates the fruit by three criteria — good for food, pleasant to the eyes, desired to make one wise — which John will recognize as the world's three temptations (1 John 2:16). The essence of the fall is not eating fruit but the human creature asserting autonomy from the Creator, claiming the right to determine good and evil independently of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 3: the serpent's lie is not that there is no God but that God cannot be trusted — that his commands are restrictions rather than gifts, and that humans can flourish better on their own terms than on his. This is the lie at the heart of every sin: that God is withholding something good. The hiding in the garden is the first evidence of a guilty conscience — conscience is the echo of God's law written on the heart, producing shame and fear before the God whom sin has offended.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the serpent was more crafty than any other beast of the field that the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, "Did God actually say, 'You shall not eat of any tree in the garden'?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The serpent is introduced as a creature — "that the LORD God had made" — not as an equal and opposite divine power. The power of evil is real but created, derivative, and ultimately subject to the Creator. Its strategy is not brute force but craftiness — the manipulation of language, the misrepresentation of God's word. "Did God actually say?" — the question subtly expands the prohibition (any tree, not one tree) and introduces doubt about whether God's word can be trusted. Waltke notes that the serpent does not deny God's existence but questions God's goodness, which is the more devastating attack: a God who withholds is not worth trusting. This is the prototype of every temptation since.

verseByVerse.quote: And the woman said to the serpent, "We may eat of the fruit of the trees in the garden, but God said, 'You shall not eat of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, neither shall you touch it, lest you die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: Eve's response adds to God's command — "neither shall you touch it" — which God did not say (2:17). This small addition is symptomatic: once the word of God becomes the object of debate rather than the foundation of life, expansions and distortions begin. Whether Eve added this to strengthen the prohibition or had simply learned it that way, the effect is that God's command is now slightly misrepresented in the conversation — making it easier for the serpent's next move. Kidner notes that entering into dialogue with the tempter on his own terms is already a step away from the safety of simple trust in God's word. Eve should have said: God has said; that is enough.

verseByVerse.quote: But the serpent said to the woman, "You will not surely die. For God knows that when you eat of it your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil."
verseByVerse.commentary: The serpent now moves from question to direct contradiction of God's word — "you will not surely die" — and then to a counter-narrative about God's motivations: God is keeping something good from you. This is the oldest and most persistent lie: that God's commands are restrictions designed to keep humanity from flourishing rather than paths that lead to flourishing. "You will be like God, knowing good and evil" — the promise contains a truth (they will know good and evil) but embedded in a lie: they will know it not as God knows it (as the sovereign source of moral reality) but as fallen creatures who discover it through guilty experience. Sproul writes that this verse contains every temptation: the rejection of God's word, the impugning of God's character, and the seduction of autonomous self-determination.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took of its fruit and ate, and she also gave some to her husband who was with her, and he ate.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three criteria govern Eve's evaluation: appetitive (good for food), aesthetic (delight to the eyes), and aspirational (desired to make one wise). John identifies these as the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16) — the architecture of worldly temptation unchanged since Eden. She took, ate, and gave — each verb a step deeper into transgression. "Her husband who was with her" — Adam is present and silent, a passive participant who receives without protest or intervention. Paul's analysis (1 Tim. 2:14) distinguishes their failures: Eve was deceived; Adam sinned with eyes open. Both ate; both bear responsibility; but the headship of Adam (addressed first by God in v.9) makes his failure the federal sin that affects all humanity (Rom. 5:12–21).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked. And they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves loincloths.
verseByVerse.commentary: The eyes are opened — but not to the wisdom the serpent promised. What they see is their own nakedness and shame. The condition described in 2:25 (naked and unashamed) is immediately reversed; the transparency of innocence has become the exposure of guilt. Fig leaves — a futile, temporary, and inadequate covering — are humanity's first attempt at self-justification: covering the symptom (nakedness) rather than the cause (sin). Every human religious and moral effort to cover guilt by self-generated righteousness is a fig leaf. Calvin notes that the shame they feel is the echo of God's law within the conscience — even fallen humans retain enough of the moral image to feel the weight of having transgressed it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they heard the sound of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. But the LORD God called to the man and said to him, "Where are you?"
verseByVerse.commentary: God walks in the garden — language of personal, intimate presence (cf. Lev. 26:12; Rev. 21:3). The "cool of the day" (ruah hayyom, literally the wind of the day) suggests the pleasant afternoon breeze — a normal time of fellowship that has now become a time of terror. They hide among the trees that were given for their blessing; the good things of creation become instruments of futile evasion. God's question — "Where are you?" — is not a request for information but a summons to account, an act of grace that calls the hiding sinner out of the dark. Keller writes that this question is the pattern of all God's gracious pursuit of sinners: he comes looking, he calls, he does not leave the rebellious in their hiding but seeks them out.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I heard the sound of you in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself." He said, "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten of the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Adam's answer reveals two dimensions of fallen humanity: fear replaces trust, and evasion replaces honesty. "I was afraid" — the first mention of fear in Scripture, born of the broken relationship with God. Fear of God in the fallen state is not reverential awe but the terror of the guilty before the holy. God's counter-question — "Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten?" — probes with surgical precision to the root: the knowledge of nakedness can only have come from the act God prohibited. The question is not a trap but a summons to honesty, an opportunity for confession that Adam will not take. Keller notes that God's questions in Genesis 3 are consistently gracious — he is not gathering evidence he lacks but drawing the sinner into the possibility of repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: The man said, "The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit of the tree, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary: Adam's answer reveals two dimensions of fallen humanity: fear replaces trust, and blame replaces responsibility. "I was afraid" — the first mention of fear in Scripture, born of the broken relationship with God. God's question — "Who told you that you were naked?" — probes to the root: the knowledge of nakedness comes from the very act God prohibited. Adam's response is a masterpiece of evasion: the woman (blame-shifting to the companion), and implicitly God himself ("whom you gave to be with me" — as if God is at fault for providing the woman). Sin not only corrupts but corrupts our ability to acknowledge corruption; self-justification is the immediate fruit of the fall, and it always involves displacing responsibility onto others.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said to the woman, "What is this that you have done?" The woman said, "The serpent deceived me, and I ate."
verseByVerse.commentary: Eve's answer is more honest than Adam's — she identifies deception as the mechanism — but still displaces responsibility to the serpent. She was deceived (1 Tim. 2:14) but not compelled; she chose to eat, and that choice was hers. The pattern of sin's aftermath is now fully established: hiding from God, fear in his presence, blame-shifting to others, and the inability to take simple, unqualified responsibility. The question "What is this that you have done?" is not rhetorical but moral — God is establishing the record of accountability before pronouncing judgment. Wenham notes that God questions each party (serpent, woman, man) in reverse order of their guilt: Adam receives the fullest judgment because his sin, as the covenant head, carries the greatest consequence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — The Curse and the Expulsion from the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The consequences of the fall are pronounced in three stages: curse upon the serpent, consequences for the woman, consequences for the man and the ground. But embedded in the curse on the serpent is the first gospel proclamation — the protoevangelium — the promise that the seed of the woman will crush the serpent's head. Judgment falls, but within the judgment is the seed of redemption.
verseByVerse.theology: The curses describe the distortion of creation's good structures: the serpent's domain is diminished, the woman's pain in childbearing and her marital relationship are disordered, the man's work becomes toil against a resistant ground, and death — already threatened — becomes the inevitable end. But these are distortions, not destructions: childbearing still happens, work still produces food, marriage still exists. Sin has corrupted but not annihilated creation's goodness. The expulsion from the garden preserves the terrible mercy of verse 22: access to the tree of life in a fallen state would mean eternal life in sin — the expulsion is judgment that contains grace.
verseByVerse.examples: The protoevangelium (v.15) is the seed from which all Messianic prophecy grows. Waltke traces the 'seed' theme through Genesis (Seth, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, David) to its fulfillment in Christ, who is the seed of the woman born under the law (Gal. 4:4) who crushed the serpent at the cross (Col. 2:15; Rom. 16:20). Calvin calls v.15 the mother of all promises — the first ray of gospel light in the darkness of the fall.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD God said to the serpent, "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all livestock and above all beasts of the field; on your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel."
verseByVerse.commentary: The serpent alone receives an unqualified curse; the woman and man receive consequences but not the word "cursed." The enmity between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed describes the cosmic conflict between the kingdom of darkness and the people of God throughout history — a conflict that reaches its climax at the cross. "He shall bruise your head" — the singular "he" anticipates one decisive representative who will defeat the serpent decisively. "Crush" (shup) — the same verb for both bruising and crushing; the serpent will wound the heel of the woman's seed (crucifixion) while the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head (resurrection and final defeat). Calvin, Waltke, and Keller all identify this as the first gospel promise: the entire redemptive history is contained in seed form in this verse.

verseByVerse.quote: To the woman he said, "I will surely multiply your pain in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The woman's consequences fall in her two primary relationships: with her children (the pain of bringing forth life) and with her husband (the distortion of the complementary relationship). Childbirth, which was to be the joyful participation in God's blessing (1:28), now carries pain. The second clause — "your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you" — is interpretively contested. Most Reformed scholars read "desire" in the light of 4:7 (same word, where sin's desire is to master Cain) as a sinful grasping for control, met by the husband's authoritative counter-assertion. The complementarity of 2:18–25 has become a power struggle. Waltke notes that the gospel does not eliminate gender difference but redeems it, restoring mutual self-giving in the place of mutual domination.

verseByVerse.quote: And to Adam he said, "Because you have listened to the voice of your wife and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in pain you shall eat of it all the days of your life; thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary: Adam's sin is named precisely: he listened to his wife rather than to God — not because listening to his wife is wrong but because he chose her voice over God's command. The consequence falls not on Adam directly but on his domain: the ground, which he was given to cultivate, now resists him. "Cursed is the ground because of you" — the creation participates in the consequence of its head's rebellion (Rom. 8:20–22). Thorns and thistles appear for the first time — the plants that will crown Jesus at his crucifixion (Matt. 27:29), suggesting that Christ's bearing of thorns is his taking on himself the curse of Adam. Work, designed as joyful cultivation (2:15), becomes painful toil against a resistant creation.

verseByVerse.quote: By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, till you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return."
verseByVerse.commentary: The mortality God warned about in 2:17 is now declared as destiny: dust you are, and to dust you shall return. This is not merely biological description but theological judgment — death is the consequence of sin, not a natural feature of God's original design. Paul builds on this verse: "the wages of sin is death" (Rom. 6:23); "sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin" (Rom. 5:12). Yet even here the curse contains restraint: the return to dust is a death, not eternal conscious torment — the worst is not yet spoken. And the ground from which man came and to which he returns is the same ground that God will use for resurrection: the one who returns us to dust will raise us from it (Job 19:25–27; Dan. 12:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The man called his wife's name Eve, because she was the mother of all living.
verseByVerse.commentary: In the midst of the curse pronouncements, Adam names his wife Eve (Havvah) — "mother of all living." This act of naming is remarkable: instead of despair or blame, Adam exercises faith. God has just promised that the woman's seed will crush the serpent (v.15); Adam names her in light of that promise. The name looks forward, not backward — to life, not to death, to the seed who will come. Wenham notes that this is the first act of faith in Scripture: Adam believes God's promise of life even as the sentence of death is being pronounced. His naming of Eve is an implicit statement: the death God warned about has not yet ended the story; life will continue, and through it the promise will come.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them.
verseByVerse.commentary: God himself provides the covering that the fig leaves could not supply. Skins require the death of an animal — the first death in Scripture, shedding blood to cover human shame. This is the proto-atonement: life given to cover the guilt and exposure of sinners. The garment of skin is more permanent and more adequate than the fig leaf of human self-justification. Kidner writes that this verse is the prototype of all substitutionary atonement: something dies so that the guilty may be covered and able to stand before God. The clothing God provides — unlike human efforts to cover shame — is sufficient because God himself is its source. Paul's language of being "clothed with Christ" (Gal. 3:27) and wearing the "garments of salvation" (Isa. 61:10) has its root here.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD God said, "Behold, the man has become like one of us in knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand and take also of the tree of life and eat, and live forever—" therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Knowing good and evil" — the serpent's promise has come true, but not as advertised. The man knows good and evil as a fallen creature, through guilty experience rather than holy wisdom. God's action in expelling them from the garden is both judgment and mercy: access to the tree of life in a fallen state would mean immortal sinners, permanently fixed in their rebellion — a kind of eternal hell without the possibility of redemption. The expulsion closes the door to immortality in sin so that the door to redeemed immortality might eventually open. Waltke writes that exile from the garden is an act of grace: God does not allow the consequences of sin to be circumvented by a shortcut, but neither does he abandon the exiled sinners — he clothes them before he sends them out.

verseByVerse.quote: He drove out the man, and at the east of the garden of Eden he placed the cherubim and a flaming sword that turned every way to guard the way to the tree of life.
verseByVerse.commentary: Cherubim — the same heavenly creatures who guard the ark of the covenant (Exod. 25:18–22) and whose images adorn the inner sanctuary of the temple — now stand at the eastern entrance to Eden, guarding the way to the tree of life. The movement is eastward: away from the presence of God, into the world east of Eden. The flaming sword that turns every way is the impassable barrier between fallen humanity and the life-giving presence of God. But the barrier is not permanent: the tabernacle and temple, with their cherubim-adorned veil, are the re-opened approach to God's presence — and Christ, who tears the veil at his death (Matt. 27:51), is the final removal of the sword. In him, the way to the tree of life is reopened (Rev. 22:2, 14).

3.theology:
The Anatomy of Sin. Genesis 3 gives the Bible's most complete account of how sin operates. It begins with doubt about the word of God (v.1), moves to distrust of the character of God (vv.4–5), leads to autonomous action against the will of God (v.6), and produces shame, fear, and broken relationship (vv.7–13). Keller identifies the root as the displacement of God from the center of life — the claim, in practice if not theory, that I am a better judge of my good than my Creator is.

The Protevangelium and Redemptive History. Verse 15 is the seed from which all of redemptive history grows. Every subsequent act of God in Scripture — the call of Abraham, the exodus, the Davidic covenant, the prophets, the incarnation — is an unfolding of this one promise. The enmity between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent is the great conflict structuring all of history, and its resolution is the cross and resurrection. To read Genesis 3 without verse 15 is to miss the point of the chapter entirely.
3.examples:
Then: Ancient Near Eastern creation-and-fall narratives — the Gilgamesh epic, the Adapa myth — portrayed sin as a cosmic accident or work of rival gods. Genesis 3 subverts them all: sin is the free act of human creatures endowed with the image of God. The curse on the ground (v.17) and painful childbirth (v.16) were daily realities for ancient Israel; Genesis 3 explained not just that these things are hard but why, and with the implication that the curse can be reversed.

Now: The fall answers what every philosophy and therapy system eventually confronts: what is wrong with us? Not ignorance, not environment, not psychology — but moral rebellion against the Creator, a structural disorder of the will requiring not improvement but redemption. The gospel begins with Genesis 3's diagnosis: we are not basically good people who occasionally do bad things, but fallen image-bearers who need a new creation. And it ends with Genesis 3's promise: the seed of the woman has come, and the serpent's head is crushed.

4.title: Am I My Brother's Keeper?
4.text: <sup>2</sup>Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground. <sup>3</sup>In the course of time Cain brought to the LORD an offering of the fruit of the ground, <sup>4</sup>and Abel also brought of the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions. And the LORD had regard for Abel and his offering, <sup>5</sup>but for Cain and his offering he had no regard. So Cain was very angry, and his face fell. <sup>7</sup>If you do not do well, sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is contrary to you, but you must rule over it. <sup>8</sup>Cain spoke to Abel his brother. And when they were in the field, Cain rose up against his brother Abel and killed him. <sup>9</sup>Then the LORD said to Cain, "Where is Abel your brother?" He said, "I do not know; am I my brother's keeper?" <sup>15</sup>And the LORD put a mark on Cain so that no one who found him would attack him. <sup>26</sup>At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD.
4.overview:
The fall of Genesis 3 moves immediately into fratricide in Genesis 4. The speed is deliberate: sin does not stay contained. Once the relationship with God is broken, the relationship between human beings fractures next, then the relationship with the ground (v.12). The spread of sin is not a trickle but a flood — and that flood is coming.

The contrast between Cain and Abel cuts deeper than jealousy. The LORD had "regard" for Abel and his offering, not for Cain's. Hebrews 11:4 says Abel offered his sacrifice "by faith," suggesting the issue was not the material offered but the orientation of the heart. Worship is always first a matter of the heart. God's gracious warning to Cain (v.7) is extraordinary: before the murder, God gives him the opportunity to see what is happening and choose differently. Cain refuses.

The chapter closes with hope in the darkness: "At that time people began to call upon the name of the LORD" (v.26). Even after murder, the human impulse toward the Creator is not extinguished. The line of Seth — those who call on the name of the LORD — will carry the seed of the woman through every catastrophe until the Promised One arrives.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Cain and Abel: The First Murder
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fall of Genesis 3 bears its first fruit in Genesis 4: fratricide. Cain and Abel are the first human brothers, and the first human murder is a brother's murder. The story moves from worship (offerings) to warning (God's counsel to Cain) to violence (the killing of Abel) to judgment (Cain cursed and exiled). The trajectory of sin — from one tree to one murder — accelerates rapidly, and the question of how fallen humanity will live east of Eden is posed in its starkest form.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between Cain and Abel is not occupational (farmer versus shepherd) but spiritual: God regards Abel's offering and not Cain's. The reason given implicitly relates to the condition of the offerer rather than the category of the gift (Heb. 11:4 says Abel offered 'by faith'). Cain's anger and downcast face reveal a heart that expected acceptance on his own terms. God's counsel to Cain — 'sin is crouching at the door; its desire is for you, but you must rule over it' — is among the most urgent pastoral words in Scripture: the battle with sin is real, personal, and winnable only by active resistance.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 4: the root of Cain's sin is the same as the root of the original fall — self-determination and the refusal to accept God's terms. Cain wants worship on his terms, brotherhood on his terms, and when denied, becomes the first murderer. The mark of Cain is both judgment (exile, wandering) and grace (protection): God does not abandon even the murderer but preserves his life. This pattern — judgment that contains mercy — runs through all of Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore Cain, saying, "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrative moves immediately from expulsion to conception: life continues east of Eden, the blessing of fruitfulness (1:28) persists despite the curse. Eve's exclamation — "I have gotten a man with the help of the LORD" — is an act of faith, acknowledging God's involvement even in the post-fall world. The Hebrew is ambiguous and has generated much discussion: some read it as Eve thinking she has born the promised seed (3:15). Whether or not Eve understood the full promise, her attribution of the birth to the LORD is significant — she does not see herself as abandoned by God but as still in relationship with the one who promised the crushing of the serpent. Life after the fall is still life given by God.

verseByVerse.quote: And again, she bore his brother Abel. Now Abel was a keeper of sheep, and Cain a worker of the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abel's birth is recorded more briefly — "and again, she bore" — without the exclamation that accompanied Cain. The two brothers represent complementary aspects of the creation mandate (1:28): cultivating the ground (Cain) and keeping animals (Abel).
