He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead.” Abraham’s obedience is grounded not in resignation but in resurrection faith: God had said the covenant would continue through Isaac; God had commanded the sacrifice of Isaac; therefore God would raise Isaac from the dead. He did not know how, but he knew who.

The theological weight of this chapter is immense. It is the most luminous prefiguration of Calvary in the Old Testament: a father, a son, a mountain (Moriah — the site of Solomon’s temple and, in Christian tradition, adjacent to Golgotha), a three-day journey, wood laid on the son’s back, the question “where is the lamb?”, and the divine provision of a substitute. The ram caught in the thicket dies in Isaac’s place; the lamb of God dies in ours. But unlike the story of Moriah, there is no angel’s hand to hold back the Father’s. The true Moriah is accomplished.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 22 is the theological summit of the Abraham narrative and one of the most profound passages in all of Scripture. God commands Abraham to offer Isaac as a burnt offering on Mount Moriah. Abraham obeys immediately and completely, proceeding to the point of raising the knife, at which moment the angel of the LORD intervenes and provides a ram as a substitute. The passage is both history and type: it is a real event in the life of a real man, and it is the most detailed Old Testament foreshadowing of the cross, in which God himself provides the sacrifice his own justice requires.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological density of the Akedah is extraordinary. It tests and reveals the depth of Abraham's faith — a faith that held the promise of resurrection (Heb. 11:19) against the command to sacrifice the promise-bearer. It establishes the principle of substitutionary atonement — a substitute provided at the moment of judgment, taking the place of the one who was condemned. It names the location 'the LORD will provide' (Yahweh Yireh), making the theology of divine provision into a permanent geographical testimony. And it is the context in which God swears the most comprehensive form of the covenant promise, now grounded in the oath of God himself.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 22: the Akedah is the passage in which Abraham's faith reaches its fullest expression — and also the passage in which the reader begins to see the shape of the gospel most clearly. The father who takes his beloved son, the three-day journey that culminates in a death-and-resurrection pattern, the wood carried by Isaac, the substitutionary ram — all these details are too specific and too theologically freighted to be coincidental. They are the shadow cast by the cross, moving backward through history. Calvin says of this passage that it is impossible to read it without being moved: a father, a son, a mountain, a knife — and a God who sees, who provides, who does not spare what is most precious.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things God tested Abraham and said to him, "Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains of which I shall tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary: "God tested Abraham" — the narrator tells the reader immediately that this is a test, not a genuine divine demand for child sacrifice. What Abraham does not know — what makes the test so severe — he must proceed without the reader's information. The triple intensification of the command — "your son, your only son, whom you love" — strips away every ambiguity: this is the covenant child, the only legitimate heir, the beloved son in whom all hope rests. "Go" — the same word (lech) as the original call (12:1): Abraham must leave everything twice, and the second leaving is harder than the first. The land of Moriah — identified in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as the location of Solomon's temple, where God will later provide the definitive sacrifice — is the destination. Waltke notes that the specificity of the command (your son, your only son, whom you love, the land of Moriah, a burnt offering) is designed to eliminate every possible alternative interpretation: God means exactly this, and Abraham's test is to obey exactly this.

verseByVerse.quote: So Abraham rose early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, and his son Isaac. And he cut the wood for the burnt offering and arose and went to the place of which God had told him. On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Abraham rose early in the morning" — the same early-rising that characterized his response to the expulsion of Hagar (21:14) and will characterize every act of obedience in his life. He does not delay, does not seek counsel, does not send for more information. He cuts the wood — the practical preparation of the one who fully intends to complete the sacrifice. The three-day journey to Moriah creates a three-day period during which Abraham lives with the intention of sacrificing Isaac: every step toward Moriah is an act of faith maintained against the natural love of a father. Hebrews 11:19 gives us Abraham's theology during these three days: he believed that God was able to raise Isaac from the dead. He held the promise and the command together by believing in resurrection. Wenham notes that the three-day journey is the most extended period of sustained, painful faith in Abraham's narrative — and that resurrection-faith is what made it possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham said to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey; I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you." And Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. And he took in his hand the fire and the knife. So they went both of them together.
verseByVerse.commentary: "We will worship and come again to you" — Abraham says "we," not "I." He speaks of both himself and Isaac returning. This is either a deliberate deception of the servants or (more likely, given Hebrews 11:19) an expression of resurrection faith: Abraham fully expects to bring Isaac back. The wood laid on Isaac's shoulders will become the most explicit Christological type in Genesis: the wood of sacrifice carried by the beloved son to the place of offering (John 19:17, Jesus carrying his cross). "He took in his hand the fire and the knife" — Abraham carries the instruments of judgment; Isaac carries the instrument of blessing (the wood for the offering that will be his salvation). The phrase "they went both of them together" — repeated in v.8 — emphasizes the shared nature of the journey: father and son proceeding together toward a destination only the father knows. Kidner writes that the image of father and son walking together toward Moriah is one of the most moving in Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaac said to his father Abraham, "My father!" And he said, "Here I am, my son." He said, "Behold, the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" Abraham said, "God will provide for himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." So they went both of them together.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's question — "where is the lamb?" — is the most theologically loaded question in Genesis. He sees the fire and the wood; he knows the offering requires a lamb; he does not see one. Abraham's answer — "God will provide for himself the lamb" — is simultaneously a statement of faith and an unconscious prophecy. He believes it because he trusts that God will resolve the contradiction between promise and command; he does not know that his words will be literally, physically fulfilled within the hour. The prophecy is more than Abraham knows: "God will provide for himself the lamb" — God will be his own provision; the lamb will be God's own offering, not Abraham's. The entire theology of atonement is embedded in this answer. "They went both of them together" — the phrase repeated, lingered over: this painful, silent, tender journey is what faith looks like when it has run out of questions and must simply walk forward. Waltke writes that Abraham's answer to Isaac is the greatest sentence he speaks in Genesis: four Hebrew words (Elohim yireh-lo haseh), a statement of radical trust, an unconscious prophecy, and the seed of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: When they came to the place of which God had told him, Abraham built the altar there and laid the wood in order and bound Isaac his son and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood. Then Abraham reached out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrative is relentlessly specific: he built, he laid, he bound, he took the knife. Each action is deliberate and specific, with no indication of hesitation. The binding of Isaac (the Akedah, from the Hebrew root akad, to bind) gives this passage its traditional name. Isaac, who is old enough to carry the wood (perhaps a young adult — Josephus says 25; some texts suggest a teenager), submits to the binding: he does not resist, does not flee, does not overpower his old father. Isaac's submission to Abraham mirrors the willing submission of Christ to the Father's will. "He took the knife to slaughter his son" — the action is complete; the intention is total. At this precise moment — the knife raised, the son bound, the sacrifice inches from completion — the angel calls. The intervention comes at the last possible instant, after faith has been demonstrated to its fullest extent. Sproul writes that this moment reveals the depth of Abraham's faith more clearly than any other: he was not testing to see if God would stop him; he was proceeding to complete the sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: But the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven and said, "Abraham, Abraham!" And he said, "Here I am." He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Abraham, Abraham!" — the double name signals divine urgency, the same doubling used at the burning bush (Exod. 3:4, "Moses, Moses") and at the Damascus road (Acts 9:4, "Saul, Saul"). God speaks at the last possible moment, arresting the act, not the intention. "Now I know that you fear God" — this does not mean God did not know before; it means that the test has produced the demonstration of what was always true. Faith that has not been tested is faith that has not been seen — by Abraham, by his community, by the watching narrative of Scripture. "You have not withheld your son, your only son, from me" — these words will echo in John 3:16: "God so loved the world that he did not withhold his only Son." What Abraham was prepared to give, God actually gave. The type and the antitype: Abraham's son is returned; God's Son is not spared (Rom. 8:32: "He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all"). Wenham notes that the verbal parallels between the Akedah and the Incarnation are too precise to be coincidental.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram and offered it up as a burnt offering instead of his son. So Abraham called the name of that place, "The LORD will provide"; as it is said to this day, "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Behold, behind him was a ram, caught in a thicket by his horns" — the provision is complete, specific, and immediately available. The ram was there before the angel spoke; God had prepared the substitute before Abraham needed it. "Instead of his son" — the most important phrase in the Akedah for the theology of atonement: the ram dies in the place of Isaac, as a substitute, taking the judgment that Isaac would have received. This is substitutionary atonement in its first and most vivid narrative form. "The LORD will provide" (Yahweh Yireh) — the name Abraham gives the mountain is a permanent testimony to what happened here. "On the mount of the LORD it shall be provided" — a proverbial saying that may anticipate the temple mount, where God will continue to provide sacrifices for the atonement of his people. Calvin writes that Moriah/Yahweh-Yireh is the theological center of the Old Testament: the mountain where God provides the substitute that his own justice requires, the mountain that will be the temple, the mountain that anticipates Calvary.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD called to Abraham a second time from heaven and said, "By myself I have sworn, declares the LORD, because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son,
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant promise is renewed in its most solemn form: God swears by himself. "By myself I have sworn" — God has no greater by which to swear (Heb. 6:13); he takes himself as his own witness, making the covenant oath as absolute and as permanent as his own being. This is the oath that Hebrews 6:13–18 cites as the foundation of the believer's confidence: two immutable things — God's word and God's oath — by which it is impossible for God to lie. The oath is grounded in Abraham's demonstrated obedience: "because you have done this and have not withheld your son, your only son." The language echoes John 3:16 in reverse — what Abraham was prepared to give, God actually gave. Waltke notes that the oath sworn at Moriah is the final, fullest form of the Abrahamic covenant.

verseByVerse.quote: I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply your offspring as the stars of heaven and as the sand that is on the seashore. And your offspring shall possess the gate of his enemies,
verseByVerse.commentary: The content of the oath: comprehensive blessing, innumerable offspring (stars and sand joined in one promise), and military victory over enemies. Stars and sand — the two greatest comparisons for innumerable multitude — are both present in this single utterance, the fullest expression of the promise of 12:2. "Possess the gate of his enemies" — military victory is part of the covenant blessing, anticipating the conquest of Canaan. The oath does not add new content to the covenant promise but seals existing content with divine self-swearing: what God has said, he now swears by himself. Kidner notes that the oath at Moriah is the moment when the covenant promise becomes humanly inviolable — secured not by Abraham's faithfulness (which has already been demonstrated) but by God's own character as the unbreakable guarantee.

verseByVerse.quote: and in your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed, because you have obeyed my voice." So Abraham returned to his young men, and they arose and went together to Beersheba. And Abraham lived at Beersheba.
verseByVerse.commentary: "In your offspring shall all the nations of the earth be blessed" — the promise of 12:3 is here sealed by divine oath and grounded in Abraham's demonstrated obedience. Paul reads "offspring" (seed, singular) as pointing to Christ (Gal. 3:16), the one through whom the blessing of Abraham reaches all nations. The Akedah is thus the moment when the gospel promise is sworn by God himself: the blessing of all nations through the seed of Abraham, secured by divine oath at the mountain where God provided the substitute. Abraham returns to his servants, and they go back to Beersheba — the site of the covenant with Abimelech and the altar to El Olam. The journey to Moriah and back is complete, and Abraham lives in Beersheba for the next period of his life. Kidner notes that the simple return to ordinary life after the Akedah is itself theologically significant: faith that has passed the supreme test returns to normal obedience, normal sojourning, normal worship — the extraordinary does not exempt the believer from the ordinary.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter concludes with a brief genealogical notice about Abraham's brother Nahor and his family. The list is not incidental; it serves the narrative purpose of introducing Rebekah (v.23, 'Bethuel fathered Rebekah') — the woman who will become Isaac's wife in chapter 24. The genealogy bridges the Akedah and the search for Isaac's wife: from the mountain of divine provision to the family that God has been preparing as the provision for Isaac's covenant continuity.
verseByVerse.theology: The placement of this genealogy immediately after the Akedah reflects the narrative logic of Genesis: the test that seemed to threaten the covenant promise is immediately followed by the report of a family that will carry the promise forward. God's provision of the ram at Moriah is followed by God's provision of a wife for Isaac — both provisions arranged before they are needed. The same divine foreknowledge that prepared the ram prepares Rebekah.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the genealogy of Nahor's family serves the structural function of transitioning from Abraham's great test (ch.22) to Sarah's death and burial (ch.23) to Isaac's marriage (ch.24) — the three episodes that will occupy the final years of Abraham's active role in the narrative. The covenant promise moves forward not through Abraham's dramatic interventions but through the ordinary biological and social processes of family life: birth, death, marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these things it was told to Abraham, "Behold, Milcah also has borne children to your brother Nahor: Uz his firstborn, Buz his brother, Kemuel the father of Aram,
verseByVerse.commentary: The genealogy of Nahor's family arrives immediately after the Akedah, as if waiting for the test to be passed before becoming relevant. "After these things" — after the covenant has been sworn at Moriah, the information needed for its continuation is provided. Eight sons from Milcah are listed: Uz (the land of Job), Buz (the land of Elihu, Job 32:2), and Kemuel "the father of Aram" connect Nahor's family to the Aramean peoples who will be Rebekah's and Rachel's homeland. The first three sons already reveal the geographical and cultural world that Isaac's covenant wife will come from. Waltke notes that the genealogical news arrives at exactly the right narrative moment: when Isaac's future needs a covenant wife, God has been growing the family that will provide one.

verseByVerse.quote: Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel."
verseByVerse.commentary: The remaining five sons complete the eight born to Milcah. But the one name that matters for the narrative's forward movement is the last: Bethuel. The narrator buries the most important name at the end of the genealogical list — a technique of narrative surprise. "Bethuel" will be the father of Rebekah (22:23), the answer to the servant's prayer in chapter 24, and the mother of Jacob and Esau in chapter 25. God has prepared the covenant wife before the covenant son's father has even begun to look for her. Kidner notes that Rebekah's introduction through her grandfather Bethuel here is itself a form of gospel: provision announced before the need is expressed, the answer growing before the question is asked.

verseByVerse.quote: Bethuel fathered Rebekah." These eight Milcah bore to Nahor, Abraham's brother. Moreover, his concubine, whose name was Reumah, bore Tebah, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Bethuel fathered Rebekah" — the sentence that the entire genealogy has been building toward. Rebekah is named here, before her story begins, as the daughter of Bethuel and granddaughter of Nahor — a full member of the covenant family of Abraham's kin. The additional four sons from Nahor's concubine Reumah complete the family picture. The total of twelve sons (eight from Milcah, four from Reumah) may mirror the twelve sons of Ishmael (25:13–15) and the twelve sons of Jacob (35:22–26) — a numerological fullness that characterizes the covenant family's generational fruitfulness. But the one name that matters for the narrative's forward movement is Rebekah: born at this moment in the text, she will be the answer to Abraham's servant's prayer in chapter 24 and the mother of Jacob and Esau in chapter 25. God has prepared the covenant wife before the covenant son's father has even begun to look for her. Kidner notes that Rebekah's introduction here is itself a form of gospel: provision announced before the need is expressed.

22.theology:
Substitutionary Atonement. Genesis 22 is the Old Testament’s clearest picture of substitutionary atonement: the ram dies in the place of Isaac, who deserved death as a member of fallen humanity. The pattern is the scaffolding on which the entire sacrificial system is built and which is finally dismantled at the cross, where the scaffold is replaced by the reality it always pointed toward. The Lamb of God does not merely provide a substitute; he is the substitute, offered by the Father, provided by himself (“God will provide for himself the lamb”).

Resurrection Faith. Hebrews 11:19 identifies the theological ground of Abraham’s obedience as resurrection faith: he “considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.” Abraham did not understand what would happen on Moriah; he trusted the character of the God who had made the impossible promise and who could be trusted to keep it even through death. This is the faith that justifies: not certainty about outcomes but trust in the character of God, who is the God of resurrection.
22.examples:
Then: Moriah is identified in 2 Chronicles 3:1 as the site where Solomon built the temple — the same mountain where Abraham offered Isaac became the place of the permanent altar of Israel’s worship. The geography is theological: the place of the ultimate act of faith became the place of the ongoing memorial of that faith, and in Christian tradition the same hill of Moriah overlooks Golgotha, where the ultimate sacrifice was offered. The mountain carries the whole weight of redemptive history on its slopes.

Now: The Akedah asks every generation the same question: is there anything you love so much that you would not give it back to God? Keller identifies this as the test of the “Isaac” in every life — the person, career, dream, or relationship that has quietly moved from gift to god. The willingness to hold even the most precious things with open hands, trusting the God who gives and takes away, is the maturity that the Akedah both requires and produces. And for the preacher, Genesis 22 is the Old Testament text that most nakedly anticipates the cross — the Father’s love that withholds nothing, the Son who carries the wood, the Lamb who is provided.

23.title: A Burial Place for Sarah
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. <sup>2</sup>And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her. <sup>4</sup>And Abraham said, “I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight.” <sup>6</sup>Hittites said to Abraham, “Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs.” <sup>17</sup>So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over <sup>18</sup>to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city.
23.overview:
Genesis 23 is the first death in the patriarchal narrative and the first property transaction in the promised land. It is given extraordinary detail — the negotiation, the cultural conventions, the precise legal transfer — because it is theologically significant, not merely biographical. Abraham buys a cave and a field at Machpelah to bury Sarah: the first piece of the promised land becomes a burial ground. The covenant people enter their inheritance through death before they enter through life.

The chapter is a study in grief and faith held together. Abraham mourns and weeps for Sarah (v.2) — genuine, public, unashamed grief. He does not spiritualize or suppress his sorrow; he enters it fully. Then he rises and negotiates for a burial place — grief that acts, that makes provision, that refuses to be paralyzed. Biblical mourning is honest emotion followed by purposeful response. The Psalms of lament follow this same pattern.

The purchase of the cave of Machpelah becomes the family tomb: Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah will all be buried there (49:29–32). It is a small plot, purchased at considerable expense, in a land still occupied by others. But it is the first concrete installment on the promise — the first piece of Canaan held in Abraham’s name. Every burial in the cave of Machpelah is an act of faith: the patriarchs choose to be buried in the promised land rather than returning to Mesopotamia, because they believe the promise of the land will be fulfilled even for their bones.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Death of Sarah and the Purchase of Machpelah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 23 records the death of Sarah at 127 years and Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah as a burial site — the first piece of the Promised Land that Abraham actually owns. The transaction is conducted with elaborate courtesy and formal legal precision, and its lengthy narration signals its importance: the purchase of Machpelah is both an act of mourning and an act of faith. Abraham insists on paying full price rather than accepting the land as a gift, creating an irrefutable legal record of his ownership of at least this piece of the land God has promised.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological significance of the Machpelah purchase is twofold. First, it is Abraham's most tangible act of faith in the land promise: he invests his own wealth in the promised land, purchasing a burial site in the land that is not yet his but will be. The purchase says, in the most concrete possible terms: I believe that my family will be here long enough to need burial land; I believe the promise enough to invest in its location. Second, the burial of Sarah in Machpelah establishes the patriarchs' permanent connection to the land: Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob will all be buried there (49:29–32), making it the physical anchor of the covenant family's connection to the land of promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham notes that the elaborate Hittite negotiation scene — with its offers of free land, its counter-insistence on purchase, its precise enumeration of the price and witnesses — reflects authentic ancient Near Eastern legal practice. The narrator's care to record every detail of the transaction is not pedantry but theology: the purchase is legally unassailable, and the legal precision is the point. When Israel returns to Canaan after Egypt, they will have clear legal title to at least this piece of land, purchased by their ancestor at full price in the presence of witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Sarah lived 127 years; these were the years of the life of Sarah. And Sarah died at Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan, and Abraham went in to mourn for Sarah and to weep for her.
verseByVerse.commentary: Sarah — the only woman in Scripture whose age at death is recorded — dies at 127 years in Hebron, the land of promise. She is 90 when Isaac is born; she lives to see him grow to manhood (37 years from birth to her death). The recording of her age honors her as a significant figure, not merely Abraham's supporting actor: she is a covenant figure in her own right, renamed by God (17:15), promised a son directly by the angel of the LORD (18:10), and celebrated in the New Testament as a woman of faith (Heb. 11:11; 1 Pet. 3:6). Abraham's mourning is real and unashamed: he goes in to mourn, he weeps. The covenant patriarch's tears over his covenant wife are a testimony to the goodness of what God has given and the grief of what death takes. Kidner notes that the record of Abraham's weeping is a reminder that faith does not eliminate grief; it holds grief within the hope of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And Abraham rose up from before his dead and said to the Hittites, "I am a sojourner and foreigner among you; give me property among you for a burying place, that I may bury my dead out of my sight."
verseByVerse.commentary: "I am a sojourner and foreigner among you" — Abraham identifies himself honestly in the first words of the negotiation. He has no legal right to permanent land ownership; he is a resident alien, not a citizen. The request for a burial site is framed as a practical necessity: "that I may bury my dead out of my sight." The ancient world's duty to bury the dead quickly and properly is the urgency behind the negotiation. Abraham does not invoke the covenant promise at this point; he approaches the transaction as a legal matter, purchasing property from the legal owners at a price they determine. This is covenant faith expressed through legal procedure: Abraham does not claim the land by the promise but purchases it through the market. Waltke notes that Abraham's acknowledgment of his sojourner status is both honest and strategically humble: he is not demanding what the promise guarantees but asking for what the law provides — and paying for it.

verseByVerse.quote: The Hittites answered Abraham, "Hear us, my lord; you are a prince of God among us. Bury your dead in the choicest of our tombs. None of us will withhold from you his tomb to hinder you from burying your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: "A prince of God among us" — the Hittites' description of Abraham is the most honorific title they could bestow: a man of divine favor, a great one, someone of exceptional standing. The pagan inhabitants of Canaan recognize what the narrative has been showing throughout the patriarchal story: God is with Abraham, and the world around him sees it. The offer is generous: any tomb they own, freely given. But Abraham will not accept free land; he insists on purchase. The reason is not false modesty but legal precision: a gift can be disputed; a purchase cannot. Abraham needs legal title, not social generosity. Wenham notes that the Hittites' offer of free land is the culturally appropriate response to a man of Abraham's standing — the principle that a great man should not need to pay for what neighbors would give freely. Abraham's refusal of this principle establishes the narrative's main point: the purchase must be legally clean and financially complete.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham rose and bowed to the Hittites, the people of the land. And he said to them, "If you are willing that I should bury my dead out of my sight, hear me and entreat for me Ephron the son of Zohar,
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham bows — the courtesy of negotiation — and makes a specific request: not any tomb but the cave of Machpelah, owned by Ephron the son of Zohar. The combination of elaborate courtesy and firm commercial specificity is the characteristic posture of ancient Near Eastern negotiation — and Abraham has mastered it. He does not ask the Hittites to give him the cave but to entreat Ephron on his behalf: he works through the social network rather than approaching the owner directly, honoring the community's role as witness and mediator in property transactions. Waltke notes that the phrase "in your midst" (implied here) signals that Abraham wants the transaction witnessed by the full community — legal precision from the first request.

verseByVerse.quote: that he may give me the cave of Machpelah, which he owns; it is at the end of his field. For the full price let him give it to me in your midst as property for a burying place."
verseByVerse.commentary: The specificity of the request — the cave of Machpelah, at the end of Ephron's field — indicates that Abraham has already identified exactly what he wants and who owns it. "For the full price" — the insistence on paying full price is repeated (also in v.13), establishing beyond doubt that Abraham's claim to the cave rests on a clean purchase, not on a gift that could be disputed later. "As property for a burying place" — the Hebrew (le-achuzat qeber) uses the word achuzah, the same word as the covenant promise of land as "everlasting possession" (17:8). A subtle connection between this commercial transaction and the larger covenant promise it partially fulfills: Abraham's purchase of Machpelah is a down payment on the covenant land. Kidner notes that the legal precision of "full price" in the presence of witnesses is Abraham's strategy for making the title to Machpelah legally unassailable.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Ephron was sitting among the Hittites, and Ephron the Hittite answered Abraham in the hearing of the Hittites, all who went in at the gate of his city, "No, my lord, hear me: I give you the field, and I give you the cave that is in it. In the sight of the sons of my people I give it to you. Bury your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: Ephron is present at the gate — the standard location for legal transactions in the ancient city. His response is the classic generous offer of the negotiation: "I give you the field and the cave." The offer is public and formal — "in the sight of the sons of my people" — but it is an offer, not a deed, and Abraham understands that accepting a gift could compromise the legal clarity of the transaction. Ephron's offer of the whole field along with the cave is significant: he is not just offering the cave but the surrounding property, which would be more valuable and which would create a larger and more complex legal gift. The generosity of the public offer may also be a negotiating tactic: by offering everything freely, Ephron makes Abraham's insistence on purchase seem even more gracious, setting up a transaction that will honor both parties. Wenham notes that the elaborate courtesy of the negotiation — both parties maximally polite, both parties working toward a known commercial outcome — is authentic to ancient Near Eastern legal practice.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Abraham bowed down before the people of the land. And he said to Ephron in the hearing of the people of the land, "But if you will, hear me: I give the price of the field. Accept it from me, that I may bury my dead there."
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham refuses the gift and insists on payment: "I give the price of the field." The public insistence on paying — made in the hearing of all the witnesses — is Abraham's legal strategy: he is creating an irrefutable commercial record in the presence of the maximum number of witnesses. The purchase will be legally unassailable because Abraham has insisted on it, Ephron has accepted it, and the entire community at the gate has witnessed it. Abraham's bowing before the people of the land is a mark of respect and gratitude that does not compromise his determination to pay. The combination of elaborate courtesy and firm commercial insistence is the characteristic posture of ancient Near Eastern negotiation — and Abraham has mastered it. Kidner notes that Abraham's insistence on paying full price is one of the most practically wise acts in his narrative: the legal title to Machpelah will be the patriarchs' most secure claim in the promised land, resting on an undeniable purchase.

verseByVerse.quote: Ephron answered Abraham, "My lord, listen to me; a piece of land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me? Bury your dead."
verseByVerse.commentary: Ephron's price — 400 shekels of silver — is considerable (David later paid 600 shekels of gold for the temple mount site, 2 Sam. 24:24; Jeremiah paid 17 shekels for the field at Anathoth, Jer. 32:9). Ephron's rhetorical dismissal of the price — "what is that between you and me?" — is a negotiating flourish that names the price while appearing to minimize it: the price stands, but Ephron's magnanimity is on display. The public naming of 400 shekels creates a fixed, witnessed price that Abraham cannot negotiate down without seeming ungrateful, and that Ephron cannot inflate afterward. Wenham notes that Ephron's price may be inflated (as some commentators suggest) or simply generous market value — either way, Abraham accepts it without counter-offer, reflecting his priority: legal title, not a bargain.

verseByVerse.quote: Abraham listened to Ephron, and Abraham weighed out for Ephron the silver that he had named in the hearing of the Hittites, four hundred shekels of silver, according to the weights current among the merchants.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Abraham listened to Ephron" — he accepts the price immediately and without negotiation. He weighs out the silver: four hundred shekels, according to the current merchant standard. The commercial precision mirrors the legal precision of the entire transaction: the correct weight, the current standard, the acknowledged market practice. No ambiguity is left anywhere in the transaction. The purchase is complete, witnessed, and commercially impeccable. Waltke notes that the phrase "in the hearing of the Hittites" confirms that the transaction has been conducted in the maximum possible publicity — the entire community at the gate has witnessed the price agreed and paid. Abraham's legal title to Machpelah is now beyond dispute.

verseByVerse.quote: So the field of Ephron in Machpelah, which was to the east of Mamre, the field with the cave that was in it and all the trees that were in the field, throughout its whole area, was made over to Abraham as a possession in the presence of the Hittites, before all who went in at the gate of his city.
verseByVerse.commentary: The legal record is complete and comprehensive: field, cave, all trees, the whole area — every element of the property specified, in the presence of the maximum legal assembly. "Made over to Abraham as a possession" — the Hebrew uses a technical legal term for formal transfer of property. The specificity of the legal description — east of Mamre, including the cave, including all trees, throughout its whole area — reflects the authentic style of ancient Near Eastern property records. Nothing is left vague; every element of what has been transferred is enumerated. This is covenant faith expressed through legal procedure: the promised land is being claimed one legally secured piece at a time. Waltke notes that the care of the legal language is the narrator's theological point.

verseByVerse.quote: After this, Abraham buried Sarah his wife in the cave of the field of Machpelah east of Mamre (that is, Hebron) in the land of Canaan. The field and the cave that is in it were made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites.
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham buries Sarah in the cave of Machpelah — his first act as the legal owner of a piece of the promised land. The location is identified twice with full geographical precision: east of Mamre, that is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Hebron will be a covenant landmark throughout the patriarchal and monarchic periods: David's first capital (2 Sam. 2:1–4). The double statement at the end — "made over to Abraham as property for a burying place by the Hittites" — is the legal summary that would appear in the ancient Near Eastern property record. Wenham notes that Abraham's ownership of Machpelah is both the smallest fulfillment of the land promise and the most legally secure: 400 shekels of silver, witnessed by all the Hittites of Hebron, unambiguously his. The covenant God fulfills his promises through ordinary, legally impeccable human transactions.

23.theology:
Grief and Faith. Genesis 23 refuses to separate genuine grief and genuine faith. Abraham mourns and weeps; he also rises and acts. The Psalms of lament demonstrate the same integration: honest expression of pain before God, followed by the refrain of trust. The New Testament does not eliminate grief but frames it differently: “we do not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thess. 4:13). The hope of resurrection does not suppress the tears of loss; it gives them a horizon. Weeping now is real; the resurrection morning will be realer.

The Pilgrim Posture. Abraham’s self-description as “sojourner and foreigner” (v.4) becomes the defining identity of the people of God throughout Scripture. 1 Peter 2:11: “I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh.” The pilgrim posture produces a particular kind of freedom: those who know they are passing through are not paralyzed by the conditions of their temporary residence. They can be generous because they are not accumulating; they can be bold because they are not protecting a permanent stake; they can love their neighbors without needing them to be their home.
23.examples:
Then: The elaborate negotiation protocol of Genesis 23 reflects the legal customs of ancient Hittite land transactions, which required public witnesses at the city gate and a formal oral and physical transfer of property. The legal precision was necessary to establish permanent ownership rather than leasehold rights. Abraham’s insistence on purchasing rather than accepting the land as a gift (vv.11–13) was strategic: a gift could be reclaimed, but a legal purchase could not. He was securing the first installment of the promise in the most durable form available.

Now: The chapter speaks to a culture that struggles with death. The modern West has largely removed death from public view, medicalized it, and deprived it of both the honest grief and the faith-framework that Genesis 23 models. Abraham mourns openly and specifically (he weeps for Sarah, not for death-in-general), then acts with faith-grounded purpose (buying a burial place in the promised land). The church that recovers the practice of honest, faith-framed grief for particular people will serve its culture better than one that either suppresses grief with spiritual clichés or drowns in it without hope.

24.title: A Wife for Isaac
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. <sup>2</sup>And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, “Put your hand under my thigh, <sup>3</sup>that I may make you swear by the LORD, the God of heaven and God of the earth, that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites among whom I dwell, <sup>4</sup>but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac.” <sup>26</sup>The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD <sup>27</sup>and said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master.” <sup>67</sup>Then Isaac brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death.
24.overview:
Genesis 24 is the longest single narrative in Genesis — sixty-seven verses devoted to the search for Isaac’s wife. The length signals the importance: the covenant must continue through the right marriage, and the right marriage requires divine guidance, faithful obedience, and patient waiting. The servant’s mission is a model of what it looks like to seek God’s leading in a specific, practical, consequential decision.

The chapter is saturated with the language of divine providence. The servant prays for a specific sign (vv.12–14), receives the sign immediately (vv.15–20), interprets it as divine guidance (v.26), gives thanks (v.27), and reports it all to Rebekah’s family as God’s own doing (vv.48–49). The word “steadfast love” (hesed) appears in verse 27 — God’s covenant faithfulness, his loyal love, his unfailing commitment — as the theological explanation for what has just happened: the right woman at the right well at the right time is not coincidence but hesed.

The chapter also contains one of the Bible’s most tender ending lines: “Isaac... took Rebekah, and she became his wife, and he loved her. And Isaac was comforted after his mother’s death” (v.67). Love and comfort in a single sentence, grief resolved in grace. This is how God works: covenant purposes fulfilled, human hearts healed, the future secured through a love that is itself a gift of hesed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Abraham's Commission to His Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 24 is the longest chapter in Genesis and one of the most carefully crafted narratives in the entire Old Testament. Its subject is the finding of a wife for Isaac — the third link in the covenant chain (after Abraham and Isaac) — and its method is the providence of God operating through the faithful prayer and discernment of an unnamed servant. The chapter is both a wonderful story of answered prayer and a theological meditation on how God guides his people through ordinary human means: conversation, hospitality, gifts, and the quiet recognitions of a seeking heart.
verseByVerse.theology: Abraham's commission to his servant is structured as a covenant charge: the servant swears by the LORD, God of heaven and earth, that he will not take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites but will go to Abraham's kin in Mesopotamia. The two negative conditions (no Canaanite wife, Isaac must not return to Mesopotamia) establish the parameters within which divine providence must work. The covenant bride must come from the covenant family; the covenant son must remain in the covenant land. These constraints are not arbitrary but theological: the purity of the covenant line and the centrality of the promised land are both at stake.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 24: the narrative of the servant's mission is one of the Bible's great stories of answered prayer. The servant prays specifically and experimentally — he asks God for a sign involving a specific action (offering water to the camels) — and the answer arrives before he has finished praying. The story teaches that specific prayer, prayed in faith, receives specific answers. It also teaches that God's guidance often operates through the recognition of his hand in ordinary events: the servant recognizes Rebecca's character through her hospitality before he knows who she is.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Abraham was old, well advanced in years. And the LORD had blessed Abraham in all things. And Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household, who had charge of all that he had, "Put your hand under my thigh,
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham is old — the covenant patriarch has reached the end of his active ministry. "The LORD had blessed Abraham in all things" — a summary of the entire covenant journey: every area of life has received the covenant blessing. The servant who receives this commission is the most trusted member of the household, the one who has charge of all Abraham has — likely Eliezer of Damascus (15:2), the servant whose potential heirship had motivated Abraham's question to God in chapter 15. Now the servant's mission is to secure the true heir's future. "Put your hand under my thigh" — the most solemn form of ancient Near Eastern oath: the hand placed near the organ of generation, invoking the covenant of procreation and the future of the family line. To swear by Abraham's thigh is to swear by the covenant promise of offspring. Waltke notes that the oath-gesture is appropriate to the mission: the servant swears by the covenant sign (procreation) to serve the covenant purpose (a wife for the covenant heir).

verseByVerse.quote: that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, among whom I dwell, but will go to my country and to my kindred, and take a wife for my son Isaac."
verseByVerse.commentary: Two negative commands and one positive: no Canaanite wife, go to Abraham's homeland, bring a wife from his kindred. The prohibition against marrying Canaanites will become a formal covenant requirement in the Mosaic law (Exod. 34:16; Deut. 7:3) — here it is a patriarchal conviction that the covenant line must be maintained through covenant family connections. The journey to Mesopotamia is both a family search and a theological act: returning to the homeland Abraham was called to leave, not to resettle there but to bring from there the person who will carry the covenant forward. Wenham notes that the two conditions — no Canaanite, go to the homeland — together define the mission's parameters in a way that makes God's guidance necessary: the servant cannot simply find a suitable woman nearby but must travel hundreds of miles to an extended family he does not know, trusting that God will identify the right person.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant said to him, "Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me to this land. Must I then take your son back to the land from which you came?" Abraham said to him, "See to it that you do not take my son back there.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's question is practical and theologically important: what if she won't come? The hypothetical opens the question of Isaac's involvement in the mission — will Abraham allow Isaac to return to Mesopotamia if necessary? Abraham's answer is immediate and absolute: no. Isaac must not return to the land of the calling. The covenant was established in Canaan; the covenant son must remain in the covenant land. His return to Mesopotamia would be a reversal of the original departure from Haran (ch.12) — the undoing of the covenant journey. Waltke notes that Abraham's absolute refusal to allow Isaac to return reflects the theological centrality of the land in the covenant: the promised land is not merely a geographical convenience but the specific place where God is working out his covenant purposes, and the covenant son must remain in that place.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD, the God of heaven, who took me from my father's house and from the land of my kindred, and who spoke to me and swore to me, 'To your offspring I will give this land,' he will send his angel before you, and you will take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman is not willing to follow you, then you will be free from this oath of mine; only you must not take my son back there."
verseByVerse.commentary: Abraham's theology of providence: "the LORD... will send his angel before you." Abraham does not know how the mission will succeed, but he knows that God who called him from Mesopotamia will guide his servant back there and send the right woman. The promise of divine guidance — "he will send his angel before you" — is Abraham's confidence, not his servant's guarantee: this is faith spoken from a lifetime of covenant experience. The release clause — "if the woman is not willing... you will be free from this oath" — is reasonable and compassionate: the servant is not bound to an impossible oath if the divine guidance he expected does not materialize. But Abraham's confidence, grounded in a lifetime of God's faithfulness, is that the woman will come. Kidner notes that Abraham's statement of divine guidance is the foundation on which the servant's entire mission rests: he goes trusting not his own skill but the God who goes before him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the servant put his hand under the thigh of Abraham his master and swore to him concerning this matter.
verseByVerse.commentary: The oath is taken. The solemn gesture — hand under thigh — and the sworn word together bind the servant to the mission. The servant's compliance with the oath procedure is itself a statement of faith: he is committing to a mission whose success depends on divine guidance he cannot see, for a woman he has not met, in a country he will travel to alone. His willingness to undertake this mission reflects the character that will be displayed throughout the chapter: he is a man of prayer, discernment, and faithful stewardship. The taking of the oath closes the commissioning scene and sends the servant on his way. Waltke notes that the servant's role in chapter 24 is one of the most positive portrayals of a secondary figure in Genesis: he is fully developed as a character — faithful, prayerful, discerning, generous — though never named. His anonymity may be deliberate: the story is not about him but about God's guidance through him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–27 — The Servant's Journey and Prayer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant travels to Mesopotamia, arrives at the city of Nahor in the evening, and pauses at the well outside the city to pray. His prayer is specific and bold: he asks God to show him the woman intended for Isaac by the sign of her offering water to his camels without being asked. He has barely finished praying when Rebekah appears and does exactly what he prayed for — not only giving him water but volunteering to water his camels as well. The servant watches in silence, wondering whether the LORD has prospered his journey.
verseByVerse.theology: The servant's prayer is a model of specific, faith-filled intercession. He addresses God as 'the LORD, the God of my master Abraham' — the covenant God who has proven faithful to Abraham — and asks for a sign that will identify the intended wife. The sign he requests is not arbitrary but character-revealing: a woman who offers to water ten camels for a stranger is a woman of extraordinary initiative, generosity, and hard work. The sign tests character, not luck. And Rebekah's response to the servant exceeds even what he asked: she runs, she fills the trough, she offers more water than the sign required.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 24:10–27: the narrative technique of this passage is masterful. The servant's prayer is answered in real time — the reader watches Rebekah arrive during the prayer, fulfill the sign, and be identified as the answer to the prayer, all in the space of a few verses. The pacing creates a sense of excited recognition: this is what answered prayer looks like, and it happens faster than the praying man could have imagined. The servant's response — silent watching, wondering, then worship — is the model of the person who has asked God for a specific sign and then watches carefully for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the servant took ten of his master's camels and departed, taking all sorts of choice gifts from his master; and he arose and went to Mesopotamia to the city of Nahor. And he made the camels kneel down outside the city by the well of water at the time of evening, the time when women go out to draw water.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant travels hundreds of miles to Mesopotamia, arrives at the city of Nahor (Haran, the homeland of Abraham's family), and positions himself at the well at the strategic time — evening, when women come to draw water. This is practical wisdom: if you are looking for women, go where women go, when they go there. The ten camels and the choice gifts signal Abraham's prosperity and the seriousness of the mission: this is not a modest inquiry but a full embassy. The servant's positioning at the well at evening is simultaneously a practical decision and a providential one: he could not have known that this was exactly the moment Rebekah would come, but God who goes before him arranged the timing. Waltke notes that the servant's arrival at the well at precisely the right moment is the first indication that the divine guidance Abraham promised has already begun to operate.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "O LORD, God of my master Abraham, please grant me success today and show steadfast love to my master Abraham. Behold, I am standing by the spring of water, and the daughters of the men of the city are coming out to draw water.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant's prayer opens with covenant language: "steadfast love" (hesed, the covenant faithfulness of God toward Abraham) is what he asks God to show. He situates himself geographically — at the spring, as the women come out to draw — and frames his request in terms of God's faithfulness to his master Abraham. The prayer is grounded in relationship, not in merit: the servant asks for God's kindness not because of his own worthiness but because of God's covenant commitment to Abraham. Waltke notes that the servant's prayer is the most carefully structured intercessory prayer in Genesis, reflecting a man who has spent his life in Abraham's household learning how to pray to the covenant God.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the young woman to whom I shall say, 'Please let down your jar that I may drink,' and who shall say, 'Drink, and I will water your camels also'—let her be the one whom you have appointed for your servant Isaac. By this I will know that you have shown steadfast love to my master."
verseByVerse.commentary: The sign is specific and character-revealing: not any woman who gives water, but the woman who volunteers to water the camels as well. Ten camels, after a desert journey, can drink as much as 25 gallons each — the volunteer is committing to an extraordinary act of labor and generosity. The sign tests character, not chance: a woman who gives that kind of service to a stranger reveals kindness, initiative, and strength that will make her an excellent covenant wife for Isaac. "By this I will know" — the servant is not being superstitious but is asking God to make his guidance visible through a specific observable action. Kidner writes that this prayer is among the most specific intercessory prayers in Scripture — a man who knows what he needs and trusts God to provide it in a recognizable way.

verseByVerse.quote: Before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah, who was born to Bethuel the son of Milcah, the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, came out with her water jar on her shoulder. The young woman was very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known. She went down to the spring and filled her jar and came up.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Before he had finished speaking" — the answer arrives before the prayer is complete. The timing is the narrative's way of expressing the immediacy and specificity of God's response: the servant is still praying when Rebekah appears. The narrator introduces her with full genealogical credentials — daughter of Bethuel, granddaughter of Milcah and Nahor, great-niece of Abraham — establishing that she meets the first criterion (from Abraham's kindred) before the servant even knows who she is. "Very attractive in appearance, a maiden whom no man had known" — her beauty and virginity are noted as appropriate for the covenant bride. She fills her jar and comes up from the spring: the servant watches. Everything is in position. Wenham notes that the genealogical precision of Rebekah's introduction serves both narrative and theological purposes: the reader knows she is the right person before the servant does, creating dramatic irony that heightens the sense of divine arrangement.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the servant ran to meet her and said, "Please give me a little water to drink from your jar." She said, "Drink, my lord." And she quickly let down her jar onto her hand and gave him a drink.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant initiates the sign-test: "please give me a little water to drink." Rebekah's response is immediate and gracious: "drink, my lord," and she quickly lets down her jar to give him water. The quickness and the title "my lord" signal the character the servant hoped to find: willing, courteous, and responsive. So far, only the first part of the sign has been fulfilled — giving water to the servant. The critical second part — volunteering to water the camels — has not yet appeared. The servant waits. Waltke notes that the servant's request for "a little water" and Rebekah's generous response echo the structure of Abraham's hospitality offer (18:3–5): the person who promises a little and gives much, or who is asked for a little and gives much, is the person whose character is revealed in the excess.

verseByVerse.quote: When she had finished giving him a drink, she said, "I will draw water for your camels also, until they have finished drinking." So she quickly emptied her jar into the trough and ran again to the well to draw water, and she drew for all his camels.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second part of the sign appears — and Rebekah exceeds it. "Until they have finished drinking" — she is committing to an open-ended task. Ten camels, after a long desert journey, can drink as much as 25 gallons each. Rebekah is volunteering to draw potentially 250 gallons of water from a well, alone, by hand. She "quickly emptied her jar" — without delay, without consulting anyone, without waiting to see if she would be thanked or paid. She runs. The character revealed by the sign is precisely what was prayed for and more: she is not merely willing but vigorous, not merely gracious but self-giving, not merely responsive but proactive. Kidner writes that Rebekah's volunteer offer to water the camels is one of the most decisive character-revealing actions in Genesis: in a single response to a stranger's small request, she shows the generosity, initiative, and energy that will characterize her entire life.

verseByVerse.quote: The man gazed at her in silence to learn whether the LORD had prospered his journey or not. When the camels had finished drinking, the man took a gold ring weighing a half shekel, and two bracelets for her arms weighing ten gold shekels,
verseByVerse.commentary: "The man gazed at her in silence" — one of the most restrained and moving moments in the narrative. The servant watches Rebekah working — drawing, running, pouring, running again — and does not speak, does not ask her name, does not interrupt the sign's completion. He is waiting to learn whether God has prospered his journey. His silence is the silence of a man watching God work, afraid to interfere with what may be the answer to his prayer. When the camels finish drinking — the sign complete — he gives her gifts: a gold nose ring and two gold bracelets. The gifts are appropriate to a woman of standing and signal the seriousness of the mission. Waltke notes that the servant's silent watching is itself an act of faith: he is trusting the sign he asked for, not acting on his own assessment before it is complete, not jumping to conclusions before God has answered.

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Please tell me whose daughter you are. Is there room in your father's house for us to spend the night?" She said to him, "I am the daughter of Bethuel the son of Milcah, whom she bore to Nahor."
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the servant speaks, asking the two questions that will complete his knowledge: whose daughter is she, and is there room for lodging? Rebekah's answer to the first question is the genealogical vindication of the entire mission: the daughter of Bethuel, son of Milcah and Nahor — Abraham's kin, exactly the family the servant was sent to find. The answer arrives before the servant asks about lodging — as if Rebekah knows that who she is matters more than what she can offer. Wenham notes that the genealogical revelation at this point — after the sign has been completed and gifts given — creates a dramatic high point in the narrative: the servant who has been watching in silence now knows that God has prospered his journey.

verseByVerse.quote: She added, "We have plenty of straw and fodder, and room to spend the night."
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah's offer of lodging is equally generous: "we have plenty" — not just enough, but plenty. The character revealed in watering the camels (generosity beyond what was asked) is confirmed in the hospitality offer (abundance, not mere sufficiency). Rebekah's responses throughout this encounter are consistent: generous, immediate, and welcoming. The straw and fodder for ten camels, plus room for the servant and his men, is a substantial offer from a young woman who has not yet consulted her household. She speaks for her family with confidence, knowing they will back the offer. Waltke notes that Rebekah's confidence in offering hospitality before checking with her family reflects the same initiative she showed in watering the camels — a woman who acts first on kindness and reconciles the details afterward.

verseByVerse.quote: The man bowed his head and worshiped the LORD and said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of my master Abraham, who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness toward my master. As for me, the LORD has led me in the way to the house of my master's kinsmen."
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant worships immediately and publicly — he does not wait to reach a designated place of prayer but bows his head right there at the well. The prayer of gratitude is structured around two divine qualities: steadfast love (hesed) and faithfulness (emet) — the same paired attributes that will define God's covenant character throughout Scripture (Exod. 34:6; Ps. 25:10; 89:14). "Who has not forsaken his steadfast love and his faithfulness" — the negative formulation acknowledges that faithfulness can appear to be forsaken (as during the long wait for Isaac) but ultimately is not. "The LORD has led me in the way" — the servant acknowledges that his arrival at the right well at the right time to meet the right woman is not coincidence but guidance. Kidner writes that the servant's worship at the well is the chapter's theological center: the entire mission rests on the steadfast love and faithfulness of the covenant God, and the man who has experienced that faithfulness worships immediately upon recognizing it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–67 — The Servant's Report, Rebekah's Consent, and the Marriage
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Genesis 24 narrates the servant's reception at Laban's house, his formal recounting of his mission and God's guidance, Laban and Bethuel's agreement to send Rebekah, Rebekah's own consent to the journey, and finally the meeting of Rebekah and Isaac at evening in the Negeb. The chapter ends with the marriage and Isaac's consolation after his mother's death. The narrative is rich with detail, theology, and human dignity — Rebekah is asked for her own consent (unusual in the ancient world), Isaac meets her in the field as he is meditating (or praying), and the marriage is described as a source of comfort to Isaac after his grief.
verseByVerse.theology: The servant's retelling of the story to Laban and Bethuel is almost verbatim repetition of the earlier narrative, slowed down to twice its length. This repetition is not literary laziness but theological intentionality: the narrator wants the reader to hear the story twice, from two perspectives, recognizing in the second telling all the divine providences that shaped the first. Laban and Bethuel's response — 'The thing has come from the LORD' (v.50) — is the Gentile household's recognition that what has happened is not merely providential but divinely arranged. The covenant God has been at work in a pagan household, preparing a covenant bride for the covenant son.
verseByVerse.examples: Rebekah's consent (v.58) is one of the most striking moments in the chapter: in an ancient world where women were given in marriage without consultation, Rebekah is asked whether she will go, and she answers immediately and decisively — 'I will go.' Her response mirrors the Abraham-type of faith: called to leave family and homeland for a man she has never met, to a land she has never seen, on the basis of a story told by a servant. Kidner observes that Rebekah's 'I will go' is the feminine counterpart of Abraham's departure from Haran — the same faith expressed in the same radical act of trust and departure.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the young woman ran and told her mother's household about these things. Laban ran out to the man to the spring.
verseByVerse.commentary: Rebekah runs home — her characteristic movement throughout the chapter is running, the physical expression of her vigorous character — and tells her family. Then Laban runs out to the well: both siblings move with urgency. The telling detail is that Rebekah tells "her mother's household" — the women's quarters of the family compound — rather than the men's quarters. The story will flow through the mother's side: Laban then goes to the man, but it is Rebekah's report that initiates Laban's welcome. Wenham notes that Laban's subsequent role — the man who calculates the value of gifts before welcoming guests — anticipates his more fully developed character in the Jacob narrative, where his mercenary instincts will create lasting conflict.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as he saw the ring and the bracelets on his sister's arms, and heard the words of Rebekah his sister, "Thus the man spoke to me," he went to the man. And behold, he was standing by the camels at the spring. He said, "Come in, O blessed of the LORD. Why do you stand outside? For I have prepared the house and a place for the camels."
verseByVerse.commentary: Laban's eagerness has a slightly mercenary quality — the text notes he "saw the ring and the bracelets" before he heard the full story — but his welcome is genuine and his hospitality is complete. "Blessed of the LORD" — Laban's greeting uses covenant language of blessing; the servant has been recognized as someone marked by divine favor. The house is prepared, the camels are provided for: Rebekah has described the servant's character and mission accurately enough that her family is ready to receive him as an honored guest. Waltke notes that "blessed of the LORD" on Laban's lips is a fulfillment of the promise of 12:3: the nations recognizing and honoring the one whom God blesses.

verseByVerse.quote: So the man came to the house and unharnessed the camels, and gave straw and fodder to the camels, and there was water to wash his feet and the feet of the men who were with him. Then food was set before him to eat. But he said, "I will not eat until I have said what I have to say." He said, "Speak on."
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant refuses to eat until he has stated his mission — an act of single-minded devotion to his purpose. Hospitality in the ancient world required that a guest eat before business was discussed: to refuse food was to signal the urgency of the matter at hand. The servant's refusal is not rudeness but covenant seriousness: he cannot rest until the mission is delivered. "Speak on" — Laban's response is gracious and curious. The servant's refusal has secured Laban's full attention; now the mission can be stated to an audience primed to listen. Waltke notes that the servant's refusal to eat mirrors Abraham's single-mindedness throughout the patriarchal narrative: some things take priority over physical needs, and covenant missions are among them.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I am Abraham's servant. The LORD has greatly blessed my master, and he has become great. He has given him flocks and herds, silver and gold, male servants and female servants, camels and donkeys.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant introduces himself and Abraham with theological precision: "the LORD has greatly blessed my master." The identification of Abraham's prosperity as divine blessing — not luck, not skill, not conquest — is the theological frame for everything that follows. The catalog of Abraham's wealth — flocks, herds, silver, gold, servants, camels, donkeys — establishes that Abraham is a man of substantial covenant blessing. This matters: the servant is coming as the representative of a prosperous covenant household, not as a poor relative seeking a charity match. Wenham notes that the servant's introduction of himself as Abraham's servant — rather than by his own name — is a mark of covenant loyalty: his identity is defined by his relationship to his master.

verseByVerse.quote: And Sarah my master's wife bore a son to my master when she was old, and to him he has given all that he has. My master made me swear, saying, 'You shall not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites, in whose land I dwell,
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant establishes Isaac's status as the covenant heir: Sarah's son, born in old age, recipient of everything Abraham has. The inheritance is total and undisputed. Then the commission is stated: no Canaanite wife. The prohibition against marrying Canaanites is both a patriarchal conviction and an anticipation of formal Mosaic law (Exod. 34:16; Deut. 7:3) — the covenant line must be maintained through covenant family connections. The purity of the covenant line is not ethnic pride but theological necessity: the line through which the promised seed will come must not be diluted by marriage to peoples whose religious practices would corrupt the household's covenant faithfulness. Kidner notes that the prohibition against Canaanite marriage is the first stated condition of the commission, establishing the theological stakes of the mission before the practical details.

verseByVerse.quote: but you shall go to my father's house and to my clan and take a wife for my son.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The positive command: go to Abraham's family in the homeland. The journey to Mesopotamia is both a family search and a theological act: returning to the land Abraham was called to leave, not to resettle there but to bring from there the person who will carry the covenant forward. The covenant bride must come from the covenant family; the covenant son must remain in the covenant land. These two constraints together define the mission's parameters in a way that makes God's guidance necessary: the servant cannot simply find a suitable woman nearby but must travel hundreds of miles to an extended family he does not know, trusting that God will identify the right person. Waltke notes that the command to go to Abraham's "father's house and clan" grounds the mission in kinship loyalty — the same loyalty that will bind Rebekah to her decision.

verseByVerse.quote: I said to my master, 'Perhaps the woman will not follow me.' But he said to me, 'The LORD, before whom I have walked, will send his angel with you and prosper your way. You shall take a wife for my son from my clan and from my father's house.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant recounts his own earlier objection and Abraham's answer — a recapitulation that serves the rhetorical purpose of demonstrating that the mission's success is not due to the servant's confidence but to Abraham's faith in God's guidance. "The LORD, before whom I have walked" — Abraham's self-description captures a lifetime of covenant relationship: walking before the God who sees and accompanies. "Will send his angel with you" — the promise of divine accompaniment and guidance, the same promise that has sustained Abraham's own journey. Kidner notes that the servant's retelling of Abraham's words to Laban's family is a form of evangelism: he is sharing the faith that motivated the mission, inviting the recipient family to see themselves as participants in a divinely arranged story.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you will be free from my oath, when you come to my clan. And if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The release clause — "if they will not give her to you, you will be free from my oath" — is reasonable and compassionate: the servant is not bound to an impossible oath if the divine guidance he expected does not materialize. But Abraham's confidence, grounded in a lifetime of God's faithfulness, is that the woman will come. The conditional structure also preserves the freedom of Laban's family: they can refuse. God's guidance does not override human freedom; it works within and through human decisions. The servant is now presenting this clause to Laban and Bethuel — implicitly inviting them to understand that their consent or refusal is a real choice with real implications. Wenham notes that the release clause, presented to Laban's family, frames their decision in terms of the servant's oath and God's guidance.

verseByVerse.quote: I came today to the spring and said, 'O LORD, the God of my master Abraham, if now you are prospering the way that I go, behold, I am standing by the spring of water. Let the virgin who comes out to draw water, to whom I shall say, "Please give me a little water from your jar to drink,"
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant recounts his prayer — virtually verbatim — as the key interpretive lens for understanding what happened. The prayer is being retold not for narrative completeness but for theological testimony: Laban and Bethuel need to understand that the servant did not identify Rebekah by his own skill or discernment but by a specific sign he asked God for. The address — "O LORD, the God of my master Abraham" — identifies the God being asked as the covenant God of a specific man: this is not a generic divine request but a covenant-grounded prayer. Waltke notes that the servant's retelling of his prayer makes Laban and Bethuel participants in evaluating the divine authentication of the mission.

verseByVerse.quote: and who will say to me, "Drink, and I will draw for your camels also"—let her be the woman whom the LORD has appointed for my master's son.'
verseByVerse.commentary: The critical element of the sign: not any hospitable woman, but the woman who volunteers to draw for the camels as well. The servant retells the sign's specification so that Laban and Bethuel understand what was asked for and what was received. "Whom the LORD has appointed" — the Hebrew (yakach, to determine, to appoint) frames Rebekah's identification not as a lucky coincidence but as a divine determination. God appointed her; the servant recognized the appointment through the sign he asked for. The logical chain is complete: sign requested, sign received, person identified, appointment recognized. Wenham notes that the servant's retelling of the sign to Laban's family is an act of spiritual transparency that invites them to evaluate the divine authentication themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Before I had finished speaking in my heart, behold, Rebekah came out with her water jar on her shoulder, and she went down to the spring and drew water. I said to her, 'Please let me drink.' She quickly let down her jar from her shoulder and said, 'Drink, and I will give your camels drink also.' So I drank, and she gave the camels drink also.
verseByVerse.commentary: The servant describes the sign's fulfillment with the same wonder that animated the original encounter: "before I had finished speaking in my heart" — the answer came before the prayer was complete. The retelling faithfully represents the miraculous speed of God's response. The full arc of the sign is recounted: request made, jar lowered quickly, drink given, camels volunteered. The quickness and the volunteering together are the sign — both elements must be present. Rebekah fulfilled both without hesitation, without being asked twice, without knowing she was being tested. Kidner notes that the servant's faithful retelling of the encounter — without embellishment or distortion — is itself a mark of the trustworthy servant: he tells the story as it happened.

verseByVerse.quote: Then I asked her, 'Whose daughter are you?' She said, 'The daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son, whom Milcah bore to him.' So I put the ring on her nose and the bracelets on her arms.
verseByVerse.commentary: The genealogical revelation — "the daughter of Bethuel, Nahor's son" — is presented as the confirmation that completed the servant's recognition: the sign revealed character (generosity); the genealogy revealed family (covenant kin).
