Jacob's response to the divine command is immediately communal: he calls his entire household to purification. "Put away the foreign gods" — Rachel's stolen teraphim (31:19), any other household gods brought from Mesopotamia, possibly Canaanite gods acquired at Shechem. The command is comprehensive: foreign gods, not just hidden gods or unused gods. Wenham notes that Jacob's command to his household is the first recorded act of covenant-household purification in Scripture — a calling of the entire community to consecration before approaching the holy God.

verseByVerse.quote: Then let us arise and go up to Bethel, so that I may make there an altar to the God who answers me in the day of my distress and has been with me wherever I have gone." So they gave to Jacob all the foreign gods that they had, and the rings that were in their ears. And Jacob hid them under the terebinth tree that was near Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary: "The God who answers me in the day of my distress" — Jacob's description of God to his household is a personal testimony: this is the God who has answered my prayers (the prayer at the Jabbok, 32:9–12), who has been with me everywhere. The testimony grounds the call to purification in Jacob's own experience: go to Bethel because the God of Bethel has proven himself to me personally. The household's compliance is total: all the foreign gods and earrings (possibly amulets or earrings connected with foreign religious practices) are surrendered. Jacob buries them under the terebinth near Shechem — not destroyed but buried, permanently inaccessible. The specific location — the terebinth near Shechem — is the place where Abraham first stopped in Canaan (12:6) and where God appeared to him. Waltke notes that the burial of the foreign gods near the terebinth of Abraham's first Canaanite encounter is symbolically rich: the covenant ancestor's site receives the burial of the foreign contamination that has accumulated in the covenant family.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they journeyed, a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob. And Jacob came to Luz (that is, Bethel), which is in the land of Canaan, he and all the people who were with him.
verseByVerse.commentary: "A terror from God fell upon the cities around them" — the divine protection that Jacob feared would be absent after the Shechem massacre (34:30: "I shall be destroyed") is actually present. God provides the protection Jacob feared his sons had forfeited: the neighboring Canaanite cities, which might have retaliated for the massacre of Shechem, are supernaturally restrained. The divine terror that prevents pursuit is the same kind of protection that operated through Laban's dream at Gilead and through the angel hosts at Mahanaim: God protects the covenant family through non-violent supernatural intervention. Jacob arrives at Bethel — Luz, the city of light, renamed the house of God — with his whole household intact. The return is complete. Kidner notes that God's provision of the protective terror is the answer to the anxiety Jacob expressed in 34:30: what Jacob feared (Canaanite retaliation) God prevents (divine terror on the cities), without Jacob needing to do anything except obey the command to go to Bethel.

verseByVerse.quote: There he built an altar and called the place El-bethel, because there God had revealed himself to him when he fled from his brother. And Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died there and was buried under an oak below Bethel. So he called its name Allon-bacuth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob builds the altar he vowed to build: El-bethel, "God of Bethel," the name that locates the God of the covenant in the specific place of the specific encounter. The altar at Bethel fulfills the vow of 28:22 — the stone pillar shall be God's house, and of all that you give me I will give a full tenth. Then an unexpected death: Deborah, Rebekah's nurse. The death of this unnamed-until-now figure is mentioned with sufficient grief to suggest she was beloved in the covenant household: the oak under which she is buried is named Allon-bacuth, the oak of weeping. Deborah has presumably been with Jacob's family since Rebekah joined it (24:59: "they sent away Rebekah their sister and her nurse"). Her death at Bethel, at the moment of covenant renewal, is the passing of the last living link between Jacob's household and Rebekah's household of origin. Wenham notes that Deborah's death at Bethel receives more commemorative detail than her life — the named burial oak preserving her memory in the landscape of covenant geography.

verseByVerse.quote: God appeared to Jacob again, when he came from Paddan-aram, and blessed him. And God said to him, "Your name is Jacob; your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name." So he called his name Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: God appears to Jacob at Bethel and confirms the Peniel name change: Israel shall be your name. The confirmation is necessary — the Peniel encounter was alone and at night, with a stranger whose identity Jacob only partly understood. Here at Bethel, in the covenant place, God himself formally declares the new name. The covenant community that Jacob leads now knows that the name change is not a private experience but a divine declaration: this man is Israel. The name confirmation at Bethel completes the circuit that began when Jacob fled to Bethel: he left as Jacob the supplanter; he returns as Israel the God-wrestler; and God confirms the new identity at the same place where the journey began. Waltke notes that the confirmation of the name change at Bethel rather than at Peniel is significant: Peniel was the moment of wrestling; Bethel is the moment of covenant formal declaration. Both are necessary: the encounter and the official acknowledgment of what the encounter produced.

verseByVerse.quote: And God said to him, "I am God Almighty: be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a company of nations shall come from you, and kings shall come from your own body. The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give the land to your offspring after you."
verseByVerse.commentary: "I am God Almighty" (El Shaddai) — the divine name that appeared to Abraham at the covenant of circumcision (17:1) and in Isaac's blessing of Jacob (28:3). The name recurs at pivotal covenant moments: the God of overwhelming provision speaking to the patriarch of the current generation. The covenant elements are all present: fruitfulness ("be fruitful and multiply," the mandate of 1:28 applied personally), national promise ("a nation and a company of nations"), royal promise ("kings shall come from your body" — anticipating David and the Davidic line), and land promise (the land given to Abraham and Isaac now explicitly given to Jacob and his offspring). The fullness of the covenant declaration to Israel at Bethel is the most comprehensive statement of the promise since the Bethel dream (28:13–15). Wenham notes that the El Shaddai declaration at Bethel completes the formal covenant transmission: Abraham received it, Isaac received it, Jacob/Israel receives it — and with his new name, the nation that will bear the covenant receives it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then God went up from him in the place where he had spoken with him. And Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a pillar of stone. He poured out a drink offering on it and poured oil on it.
verseByVerse.commentary: "God went up from him" — the divine departure signals the close of the theophany. Jacob's response is the same as at the first Bethel encounter: a pillar, oil. But now there is an addition: a drink offering. The drink offering (a libation of wine or oil) is a more developed liturgical act than the simple anointing of the first Bethel pillar — Jacob's worship has matured. The pillar at the second Bethel encounter is the fulfillment of the vow of 28:22: "this stone, which I have set up for a pillar, shall be God's house." The vow is now fulfilled; the stone stands; the oil is poured. Twenty years of covenant journey, from flight to return, from Jacob to Israel, from a stone pillow to a consecrated pillar — the circle is complete. Waltke notes that the addition of the drink offering at the second Bethel pillar reflects Jacob's liturgical development: he began with the basic act of anointing a stone; he returns with a more complete act of worship that includes both oil and libation.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob called the name of the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Bethel — house of God — is named again by Jacob. The name given at the first encounter (28:19) is confirmed at the second. The re-naming is not a contradiction but a covenant confirmation: this place is still and always the house of God, the site of the two greatest divine encounters of Jacob's life. The double naming of Bethel by Jacob frames his entire covenant journey: he named it when he fled, alone with a stone pillow; he names it again when he returns, with a household of twelve sons and two daughters, having encountered God at Peniel and been transformed. The place is the same; Jacob is not. Kidner writes that Jacob's renaming of Bethel at the end of his covenant journey back to Canaan is the narrative closure of the Bethel vow: the vow made in fear, the fulfillment achieved through grace, and the place renamed in gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they journeyed from Bethel. When they were still some distance from Ephrath, Rachel went into labor, and she had hard labor. And when her labor was at its hardest, the midwife said to her, "Do not fear, for you have another son."
verseByVerse.commentary: Rachel's labor begins on the road south from Bethel — and it is hard labor, the hardest she has endured. The midwife's comfort — "do not fear, for you have another son" — is the comfort of a woman who knows the mother is dying but can at least give her the news she has most longed to hear: another son. Rachel prayed desperately for sons (30:1: "give me children, or I shall die!"); the ironic fulfillment is that she receives the second son she hoped for at the cost of the very life she threatened to lose without them. The midwife's "do not fear" echoes the divine "do not fear" given to patriarchs in moments of covenant crisis (15:1; 21:17; 26:24; 28:13) — but here the comfort is human and the fear is mortal. Waltke notes that Rachel's death in childbirth is one of the most poignant reversals in Genesis: the woman whose hunger for children defined her narrative dies bringing a child into the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And as her soul was departing (for she was dying), she called his name Ben-oni; but his father called him Benjamin. So Rachel died, and she was buried on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).
verseByVerse.commentary: "As her soul was departing" — the narrator watches Rachel die in a single phrase of terrible gentleness. Her name for the son is Ben-oni — "son of my sorrow" or "son of my strength": the name of a dying mother's last breath. Jacob renames him Benjamin — "son of the right hand" or "son of the south": a name of favor and strength rather than sorrow. Jacob will not name his last son for Rachel's dying pain. The renaming is both mercy (the child will not carry the name of his mother's death) and covenant hope (the right hand is the place of power and favor). Rachel is buried at the side of the road near Bethlehem — not in the cave of Machpelah with Abraham and Sarah and Isaac and Rebekah and Leah (49:31), but alone, on the road, in a roadside grave. The rabbis and later interpreters (Jer. 31:15) will find deep significance in Rachel's roadside grave: she weeps for her children as they pass by on the road to exile. Kidner writes that Rachel's burial on the road is the most poignant geographical detail in Genesis: the beloved wife, the longed-for children, buried alone on the journey.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob set up a pillar over her tomb. It is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which is there to this day. Israel journeyed on and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob sets up a pillar over Rachel's tomb — the same pillar-setting that has marked every covenant and encounter site in his journey. For Bethel: a pillar. For the covenant with Laban: a pillar heap. For the reunion with Esau: no pillar (the relationship needed no monument). For Rachel's tomb: a pillar. The pillar over Rachel's grave is the monument of grief and love — Jacob mourning his most loved wife with the same gesture he uses to mark his most significant divine encounters. "It is the pillar of Rachel's tomb, which is there to this day" — the narrator connects his present to Jacob's past: the pillar endures as a permanent memorial. "Israel journeyed on" — the name Israel now used consistently for the patriarch, the life that continues after the most painful loss. The covenant family cannot stop for grief; the journey continues. Wenham notes that the transition from "Jacob set up a pillar" to "Israel journeyed on" in consecutive sentences is the chapter's most compressed portrait of grief and faithfulness: grief is real; the covenant journey continues.

verseByVerse.quote: While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine. And Israel heard of it. Now the sons of Jacob were twelve. The sons of Leah: Reuben (Jacob's firstborn), Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun;
verseByVerse.commentary: Reuben's violation of Bilhah — Jacob's concubine and Rachel's servant — is reported without elaboration: one sentence, then "Israel heard of it," then the list of twelve sons. The act is a political and sexual crime: lying with a father's concubine was a claim to the father's position and inheritance (cf. Absalom's violation of David's concubines, 2 Sam. 16:21–22). Reuben, the firstborn, is claiming a position not yet given to him. Jacob hears and does not act immediately — the delayed response will come in the dying blessing of chapter 49, when Jacob strips Reuben of the firstborn's priority (49:3–4). The transition to the list of twelve sons immediately after the Reuben notice is jarring and intentional: the covenant promise of a nation (35:11) is fulfilled in the twelve sons, even as the moral failures that will complicate that nation's origins are being recorded. Waltke notes that the list of twelve sons following Reuben's sin is the narrator's way of holding together the covenant promise and the covenant family's moral failure.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin; the sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali;
verseByVerse.commentary: Rachel's sons — Joseph and Benjamin — stand together in the list: the two sons of the most loved wife, born at such cost (Joseph after years of barrenness; Benjamin at the cost of Rachel's life). Dan and Naphtali from Bilhah follow: the two sons who were born to Jacob through Rachel's surrogate strategy, the ones through whom Rachel felt she was "prevailing" in the competition with Leah (30:6, 8). The four sons associated with Rachel — two biological, two through Bilhah — constitute the part of the twelve tribes most directly connected to Jacob's love for Rachel. Wenham notes that the listing of sons by mother preserves the household structure that produced the twelve tribes, acknowledging the complex domestic history that lies behind the clean numerical completeness of twelve.

verseByVerse.quote: the sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
verseByVerse.commentary: Gad and Asher from Zilpah complete the twelve. The note that these were born "in Paddan-aram" is a narrative summary rather than strict geography — Benjamin was born in Canaan (35:18), not Paddan-aram — but it serves the structural purpose of connecting the twelve to the Mesopotamian sojourn where most of them were born. The symmetry of the four groups — two sons from each of the two servants, six from Leah, two from Rachel — is the covenant household's structure permanently established as the nation's foundation. Waltke notes that the list of twelve at this point in the narrative is the covenant promise's fulfillment in miniature: the nation promised to Abraham (12:2; 17:4) exists, in seed form, in the twelve sons of Jacob whose names will become the names of Israel's twelve tribes.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, or Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had sojourned. Now the days of Isaac were 180 years.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob arrives at Mamre — Hebron, the site of Abraham's covenant presence and of the cave of Machpelah (ch.23). He arrives to find his father Isaac still alive: the father he left behind twenty years ago, who expected to die before Jacob left (27:2), is still living. The reunion of father and son, after Jacob's long sojourn, is not narrated at length — the narrator simply notes the arrival at Mamre and then records Isaac's age: 180 years. The age implies that Isaac is near death. Jacob, who spent twenty years away from his father, arrives in time to be present at his father's death. The covenant continuity that skipped a generation — Jacob received the covenant from God directly rather than from Isaac — is restored in this quiet homecoming. Wenham notes that Jacob's arrival at Mamre to find Isaac still alive is one of Genesis's quiet surprises: the man who thought he was dying at the time of the blessing (27:2) lives another twenty years after Jacob's departure.

verseByVerse.quote: And Isaac breathed his last, and he died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Isaac's death at 180 years is described with the same dignified formulas as Abraham's (25:8: "full of years") and Ishmael's (25:17: "gathered to his people"): a good death, a full life, a peaceful ending. The detail that "his sons Esau and Jacob buried him" echoes the burial of Abraham by "Isaac and Ishmael his sons" (25:9): the covenant heir and the non-covenant heir come together at the patriarch's death. As Isaac and Ishmael were reconciled in burying Abraham, Esau and Jacob are reconciled in burying Isaac. The covenant patriarch who received the promise from Abraham and passed it to Jacob is gathered to his people; the promise lives on in Jacob and his twelve sons. Kidner writes that Isaac's burial by both sons is the chapter's final image of covenant and grace: the brothers who were separated by the stolen blessing are reunited by their father's death, performing together the last act of filial love.

35.theology:
Genesis 35’s command to “put away the foreign gods” is the Old Testament template for the ongoing work of sanctification. The household of Jacob has carried idols from Haran (Rachel’s teraphim), accumulated jewelry of uncertain provenance, and tolerated religious syncretism. The call to Bethel is the call to decisive renunciation—not gradual diminishment of the old life but burial of it. The Pauline counterpart is the same: “Put off your old self” (Eph 4:22)—the same decisive language of burial and replacement.

Rachel’s death at Bethlehem is a theological anticipation. The place of weeping becomes the place of birth (Benjamin), the city of David, and ultimately the birthplace of the Son of David. The pilgrim’s road through sorrow and death does not bypass Bethlehem; it runs through it. Keller often notes that the gospel does not remove suffering from the path but transforms what suffering means: it is the road to glory, not the interruption of it (Rom 8:17–18).
35.examples:
Jacob’s spiritual leadership in verses 1–5 is the first sustained leadership initiative we see from him. He gathers the household, commands the purification, collects and buries the idols, and leads them up to Bethel. The Jabbok has done its work: the man who manipulated his family is beginning to lead them. The transformation is not complete—he will still show favoritism to Joseph—but the direction has changed. Suffering, faithfully received, produces the fruits of leadership that comfort never could.

Benjamin’s renaming from “son of my sorrow” to “son of my right hand” is a small act of grace in the moment of grief. Jacob does not deny Rachel’s sorrow or his own; he refuses to let it be the child’s permanent identity. The pastoral instinct to rename grief without erasing it—to speak of the resurrection without minimizing the death—is modeled here. Sorrow is real; it is not the final word.

36.title: The Generations of Esau
36.text: These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom). Esau took his wives from the Canaanites: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite, and Basemath, Ishmael’s daughter, the sister of Nebaioth. ... Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock, all his beasts, and all his property that he had acquired in the land of Canaan. He went into a land away from his brother Jacob. For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. The land of their sojournings could not support them because of their livestock. So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom. ... These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. ... These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites.
36.overview:
Genesis 36 is the Esau genealogy—thirty-three verses of names, clans, chiefs, and kings. Modern readers often skim it; the ancient reader would have understood it as a theological statement of enormous significance. Esau’s line becomes the nation of Edom, with kings and chiefs in abundance, before Israel has a single king. The line that was passed over for covenant blessing nevertheless flourishes in the world. God’s non-election of Esau is not his destruction.

The placement of the Edom genealogy is structurally significant: it closes out the Esau story before the Joseph narrative begins. Genesis consistently disposes of secondary lines (Ishmael in 25, then Esau here) before focusing on the covenant line. The pattern signals narrative priority, not divine indifference—Esau’s descendants are honored with a full genealogy, kings and all.

Theologically, the kings of Edom (vv.31–39)—a list of eight kings, each one dying and being succeeded by a non-son—anticipate Israel’s royal history. Edom has kings before Israel; Israel will eventually have kings too. The note that these kings reigned “before any king reigned over the Israelites” is a quiet forward glance at Saul, David, and all who follow. God’s purpose for Israel runs through a different kind of king than Edom’s.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 36 is entirely devoted to the descendants of Esau — his wives, sons, chiefs, and the kings of Edom who reigned before any king reigned in Israel. The chapter is the most extensive genealogy in the patriarchal narratives, reflecting the importance of Edom as a neighboring nation throughout Israel's history. Like the Ishmael genealogy of chapter 25, the Esau genealogy serves the covenant purpose of completing the account of Abraham's non-covenant descendants before the narrative focuses exclusively on the covenant line through Jacob.
verseByVerse.theology: The theological function of the Esau genealogy is both retrospective and anticipatory. Retrospectively, it fulfills the covenant promises made to Esau: the word of Isaac (27:39–40) and the promises associated with Esau's line (the nations associated with him) are seen to be fulfilled in the extensive and politically organized Edomite people. Anticipatorily, it establishes the nation that will be Israel's perpetual neighbor and frequent adversary — the nation against which the prophets (Obadiah, Isaiah 34, Jeremiah 49, Ezekiel 35) will pronounce oracles of judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: Wenham on Genesis 36: the Esau genealogy demonstrates that the covenant promise of numerous offspring and national stature is not limited to the elect line. Esau, whose descendants become Edom with kings and chiefs before Israel has any king, receives a form of covenant fruitfulness — the fruitfulness of common grace. God is generous to the non-elect line; the covenant promise's overflow benefits even those who despised the birthright. The chapter is a reminder that God's grace is not confined to the narrow channel of election but flows broadly into the created world.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Esau (that is, Edom). Esau took his wives from the Canaanites: Adah the daughter of Elon the Hittite, Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite,
verseByVerse.commentary: The toledoth of Esau opens his genealogy — the same formula used for the covenant patriarchs (Isaac, 25:19; Jacob, 37:2). Esau receives the same genealogical honor as his brother, though the content of his genealogy is entirely outside the covenant line. His wives from Canaan are named: Adah from the Hittites, Oholibamah from the Hivites. These are the same Canaanite marriages that caused grief to Isaac and Rebekah (26:34–35) and motivated Jacob's mission to Paddan-aram (28:1). Esau's Canaanite wives are not presented here as a moral failure but as the historical fact that shaped the character of his descendants: the Edomites are a mixed people, combining Esau's Semitic heritage with Canaanite culture and geography. Waltke notes that the opening of the Esau genealogy with his Canaanite wives is the narrative explanation for Edom's character as a nation: they are the descendants of the man who valued the present over the covenant, and their wives reflect that same immediate-value orientation.

verseByVerse.quote: and Basemath, Ishmael's daughter, the sister of Nebaioth. Adah bore to Esau, Eliphaz; Basemath bore Reuel;
verseByVerse.commentary: Basemath from Ishmael's family — the wife Esau took after learning that Canaanite wives displeased his father (28:9, where she is called Mahalath). The third wife connects Esau to both the Canaanite world (through his first two wives) and to the broader Abrahamic family (through Ishmael's daughter). Eliphaz from Adah and Reuel from Basemath are the first named sons. Eliphaz will become the father of Teman — a region and people associated with wisdom (Job's friend Eliphaz the Temanite, Job 2:11; the wisdom of Teman mentioned in Jer. 49:7). The beginning of Edom's genealogy already anticipates the wisdom tradition associated with Edomite/Temanite culture, a tradition that will influence the book of Job. Wenham notes that the identification of Esau's wives and sons with specific Canaanite and Arabian groups is not merely genealogical but geopolitical: these names map the territories and peoples of the ancient Near Eastern world that will interact with Israel throughout its history.

verseByVerse.quote: and Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of Canaan. Then Esau took his wives, his sons, his daughters, and all the members of his household, his livestock, all his beasts, and all his property that he had acquired in the land of Canaan. He went into a land away from his brother Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary: Oholibamah's three sons complete the initial list of Esau's five sons — one from each of his wives plus three from Oholibamah. Then the departure: Esau takes his entire household, livestock, and property and moves away from Jacob. The departure echoes the separation of Lot from Abraham (13:11): two men with too much livestock for the land to support both of them, separating to give each room to grow. The departure is peaceful and final: Esau moves to Seir, establishing the geographical separation that will define Edomite and Israelite identity for centuries. "Away from his brother Jacob" — the narrative's summary of what Esau's departure means: the Esau and Jacob story, which began in the womb, ends with a quiet and permanent geographical separation. Waltke notes that Esau's departure from Canaan, like Lot's departure to the east of Canaan, creates the geographic space for the covenant family to develop in the promised land without fraternal competition.

verseByVerse.quote: For their possessions were too great for them to dwell together. The land of their sojournings could not support them because of their livestock. So Esau settled in the hill country of Seir. Esau is Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary: The same reason given for the separation of Abraham and Lot (13:6: "the land could not support both of them") applies here: too much livestock for shared territory. The blessing of abundant livestock — the covenant blessing that operated on Jacob's labor in Laban's household — has overflowed into prosperity that makes cohabitation impossible. Esau settles in the hill country of Seir — the rugged, elevated terrain south and east of the Dead Sea that will be Edom's permanent homeland. "Esau is Edom" — the equation is the chapter's central identifier: Esau the person becomes Edom the nation. The transformation of the individual into the national is the theme of the entire Genesis narrative: Abraham becomes a covenant family, Jacob becomes Israel, Esau becomes Edom. Kidner notes that the equation of Esau and Edom is the genealogy's theological purpose: understanding Edom requires understanding Esau, and understanding Esau requires understanding the choices he made at the birthright, the Canaanite marriages, and the departure from Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the generations of Esau the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir. These are the names of Esau's sons: Eliphaz the son of Adah the wife of Esau, Reuel the son of Basemath the wife of Esau.
verseByVerse.commentary: A second toledoth formula introduces the more detailed genealogy of Esau's descendants: "the father of the Edomites in the hill country of Seir." The location is now fixed: Seir is Edom's homeland, and Esau is Edom's founding father. The sons are listed again with their mothers: Eliphaz from Adah, Reuel from Basemath — establishing the maternal line that will determine the genealogical connections of the subsequent list of chiefs. The double toledoth (vv.1 and 9) for Esau mirrors the double toledoth for Ishmael (25:12 and 16) and reflects the editorial care of the final form of Genesis: the non-covenant lines receive full genealogical treatment, not dismissal. Wenham notes that the repetition of the genealogical headings is characteristic of the Priestly genealogical tradition in Genesis, which tends to restate the framework before adding detail — a form of the literary device of resumptive repetition.

verseByVerse.quote: The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz. (Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son; she bore Amalek to Eliphaz.) These are the sons of Adah, Esau's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary: Eliphaz's sons include Teman — the region associated with Edomite wisdom (Eliphaz the Temanite in Job 2:11) — and Amalek from the concubine Timna. The Amalekites, descended from Eliphaz through Timna, will become Israel's first and most persistent military enemy after the Exodus (Exod. 17:8–16; Deut. 25:17–19; 1 Sam. 15). The genealogy traces the ancestry of Israel's future adversaries to the specific family relationships within Esau's line. Amalek, born of a concubine (not a wife), occupies a secondary position within Eliphaz's family — but the secondary position in the genealogy does not diminish the historical significance of the people who will bear his name. Waltke notes that the parenthetical introduction of Timna and Amalek is the genealogy's way of preserving the historical memory that Israel's most dangerous early enemy was a cousin-nation, descended from Esau through Eliphaz.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon, Esau's wife: she bore to Esau Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
verseByVerse.commentary: Reuel's sons — Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, Mizzah — complete the sons of Basemath's line. Shammah and Zerah will be recognizable names in later Edomite and Israelite contexts. Oholibamah's three sons (already listed in v.5) are restated: Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. The repetition serves the genealogical purpose of cross-referencing: the reader now has each of Esau's five sons listed with their mothers and their sons, creating a complete two-generation picture of Esau's immediate family before the chapter moves to the political organization of Edom as chiefs and kings. Wenham notes that the genealogical detail of chapter 36 — far more extensive than any other non-covenant genealogy in Genesis — reflects the significance of Edom as a nation that will interact with Israel throughout its history, from the Exodus refusal (Num. 20:14–21) to the Davidic conquest (2 Sam. 8:14) to the prophetic condemnation (Obadiah).

verseByVerse.quote: These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau. The sons of Eliphaz the firstborn of Esau: the chiefs Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz, Korah, Gatam, and Amalek; these are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Adah.
verseByVerse.commentary: The "chiefs" (alluf, literally "one of a thousand," a clan-leader or chief) represent the political structure of early Edom: not a monarchy but a confederation of tribal chiefs. Each son of Esau becomes a chief over his own clan. The Eliphaz chiefs — seven names including Amalek — map the political geography of early Edom: each name corresponds to a region or people-group within the territory Esau's descendants have settled. The recitation of chiefs after the genealogy of sons reflects the transition from family history to national history: Esau's sons have become clan-chiefs, and their clans have become the building blocks of the Edomite nation. Waltke notes that the political organization of Edom as a confederation of chiefs before the monarchy period reflects an authentic picture of early second-millennium tribal organization in the ancient Near East — the genealogical data is historically plausible.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Reuel, Esau's son: the chiefs Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah; these are the chiefs of Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath, Esau's wife. These are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau's wife: the chiefs Jeush, Jalam, and Korah; these are the chiefs of Oholibamah the daughter of Anah, Esau's wife.
verseByVerse.commentary: The remaining chiefs from Reuel's and Oholibamah's lines complete the enumeration. The total is fourteen chiefs from Esau's five sons — a number that creates the same comprehensive enumeration as the twelve sons of Jacob and the twelve princes of Ishmael. The Edomite nation, at its founding, has fourteen clan-chiefs organized around the three groups of wives: Adah's line (seven chiefs through Eliphaz), Basemath's line (four chiefs through Reuel), and Oholibamah's line (three chiefs from her sons directly). The structural symmetry of the lists suggests careful preservation of genealogical records that the narrator incorporates into the covenant story to give Edom its proper historical weight. Kidner notes that the comprehensive enumeration of Edomite chiefs in chapter 36 is the genealogical equivalent of the table of nations in chapter 10: it maps the political world that Israel will inhabit.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Esau (that is, Edom), and these are their chiefs. These are the sons of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom.
verseByVerse.commentary: The narrative shifts from Esau's descendants to the Horites — the pre-Edomite inhabitants of Seir whom Esau's descendants displaced (Deut. 2:12, 22: "the sons of Esau dispossessed the Horites and settled in their place"). The Horite chiefs are listed: seven sons of Seir who organized the earlier population of the same territory. The intertwining of Esau's genealogy with the Horite genealogy reflects the historical complexity of Edom's origins: the Edomites did not arrive in an empty land but displaced an existing population, and the two peoples intermarried (Oholibamah, Esau's wife, is the daughter of Anah the Horite, v.25). The listing of the Horites is the genealogy's acknowledgment of the pre-Edomite inhabitants of Seir — the archaeology of the land before Israel's neighbor arrived. Wenham notes that the inclusion of the Horite genealogy in Esau's toledoth is one of the most historically sophisticated moments in Genesis, reflecting the narrator's awareness that national origins are complex and involve displacement of prior inhabitants.

verseByVerse.quote: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in the land of Edom. The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan's sister was Timna.
verseByVerse.commentary: Lotan's sons include Hori — possibly the eponymous ancestor of the Horites themselves — and the note that Lotan's sister was Timna. Timna is the same Timna who became Eliphaz's concubine and bore Amalek (v.12): the genealogy creates the link between the Horite and Edomite populations through this one woman who appears in both family trees. Timna's dual appearance — as the sister of Lotan the Horite and as the concubine of Eliphaz the Edomite — represents the intermarriage between the displaced population (Horites) and the displacing population (Edomites) that made Edom a mixed people. The genealogical detail is historically plausible and theologically significant: the nations of the ancient Near East are not racially pure but are the product of migration, conquest, intermarriage, and cultural mixing that the genealogies carefully track. Waltke notes that Timna's genealogical function — connecting Horite and Edomite through her person — is one of the genealogy's most elegant structural moves.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah; he is the Anah who found the hot springs in the wilderness, as he pastured the donkeys of Zibeon his father.
verseByVerse.commentary: Shobal's five sons and Zibeon's two sons continue the Horite genealogy. The parenthetical note about Anah — that he found the hot springs (or mules, the Hebrew yemim is debated) in the wilderness while pasturing donkeys — is one of the most unexpected details in Genesis: a genealogy pausing to record a discovery. Whether "hot springs" or "mules" (the two main readings of yemim), the note preserves the memory of a specific act of Anah that was remarkable enough to be recorded. The inclusion of this practical detail in the midst of a formal genealogy is characteristic of Hebrew narrative: genealogies are not merely lists but repositories of memory, preserving the distinctive acts and characteristics of ancestors alongside their names. Kidner notes that the Anah parenthesis is a reminder that the genealogies of Genesis are not abstract constructs but records of real people who lived, worked, discovered, and were remembered for specific acts.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah the daughter of Anah. These are the sons of Dishon: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
verseByVerse.commentary: Anah's children include Oholibamah — confirming the identification of Esau's wife as the daughter of this specific Anah (the Horite), resolving the apparent discrepancy between v.2 (Oholibamah daughter of Anah son of Zibeon) and the Horite genealogy. The genealogy is self-consistent: Oholibamah is a Horite woman, daughter of Anah, granddaughter of Zibeon, who married Esau. The intermarriage of Esau with Horite women (Oholibamah) is not incidental but constitutive of Edom's mixed identity. Dishon's four sons continue the Horite enumeration. The name Hemdan (or Hamran in 1 Chr. 1:41) appears only here; these names preserve the memory of Horite clans that have left no other historical record. Wenham notes that the Horite genealogy's function is to map the pre-Edomite world of Seir — the people whose land Esau's descendants occupied — with the same genealogical care given to the covenant family.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final Horite chiefs and their sons complete the enumeration. Ezer's sons — Bilhan, Zaavan, Akan — and Dishan's sons — Uz and Aran — bring the Horite genealogy to its conclusion. Uz — a name that appears here, in the Nahor genealogy (22:21), and in the setting of Job ("the land of Uz") — is one of the genealogy's connections to the wider ancient Near Eastern world that the patriarchal narratives inhabit. The geographic and ethnic range of these names — from Horite clans in Seir to Arabian peoples to the setting of Israel's greatest wisdom poem — demonstrates the interconnectedness of the ancient world that the Genesis genealogies preserve. Waltke notes that the completion of the Horite enumeration with Uz and Aran is the genealogy's way of acknowledging that the land of Edom has a pre-Edomite history that the covenant narrative respects and records.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the chiefs of the Horites: the chiefs Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan; these are the chiefs of the Horites, chief by chief in the land of Seir.
verseByVerse.commentary: The summary list of Horite chiefs mirrors the summary list of Edomite chiefs (vv.15–18): seven Horite chiefs, organized by name and title. The formal conclusion — "chief by chief in the land of Seir" — is the genealogy's acknowledgment that the Horites were a politically organized people with a territorial claim to Seir before the Edomites arrived. The parallel structure of the Edomite and Horite chief-lists (each organized as a formal enumeration with a concluding summary) reflects the narrator's equal respect for both peoples: both were real nations, both were politically organized, both inhabited the land of Seir in different periods. The historical conscience of the Esau genealogy is one of its most striking characteristics: it does not simply celebrate Esau's descendants but acknowledges the prior inhabitants of the land they came to occupy. Kidner notes that the careful preservation of the Horite genealogy alongside the Edomite is an act of historical honesty that is characteristic of the best moments of the Genesis narrative.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom, before any king reigned over the Israelites. Bela the son of Beor reigned in Edom, the name of his city being Dinhabah.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Before any king reigned over the Israelites" — the note is the theological hinge of the king-list: Edom had kings before Israel had any. The contrast is deliberate and pointed. The nation that Israel will encounter throughout its history — sometimes as enemy, sometimes as neighbor — was politically advanced enough to have a monarchy before Israel's monarchy even began. Esau's despised birthright has nonetheless produced a nation with kings; Jacob's covenant birthright will eventually produce a nation with kings, but later. The first Edomite king — Bela son of Beor from Dinhabah — is a historical figure whose name and city are recorded. Bela son of Beor is sometimes linked by commentators to Balaam son of Beor (the prophet hired by Balak in Num. 22), though the identification is uncertain. Waltke notes that the Edomite king-list is the most politically sophisticated section of the Esau genealogy, reflecting a period when Edom had a functioning monarchy while the covenant family was still a semi-nomadic clan.

verseByVerse.quote: Bela died, and Jobab the son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place. Jobab died, and Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary: The succession of kings — Bela, then Jobab, then Husham — follows a pattern unique in the ancient world: there is no indication that the kingship was hereditary. Each king "died" and was succeeded by a king from a different family or location. The Edomite monarchy appears to have been elective or confederate rather than dynastic — a different political structure from the hereditary dynasties of Egypt, Mesopotamia, and eventually Israel. Bozrah — Jobab's city — will become the most prominent city of Edom in prophetic literature (Isa. 34:6; 63:1; Jer. 49:13, 22; Amos 1:12). The Temanites — Husham's people — are the wise men of Edom, associated with the wisdom tradition that will produce Job's friend Eliphaz. The king-list maps the cultural geography of Edom through its royal succession. Wenham notes that the non-dynastic character of the Edomite kingship preserved in the list is historically plausible and distinctive: early Edom appears to have been a confederacy of tribal chiefs that periodically elevated one of their own to royal status without establishing a royal family.

verseByVerse.quote: Husham died, and Hadad the son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, reigned in his place, the name of his city being Avith. Hadad died, and Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary: Hadad son of Bedad is the most historically significant of the early Edomite kings: he defeated Midian in the country of Moab — a military campaign that demonstrates Edom's regional power in the period before Israel's monarchy. The defeat of Midian in Moab establishes Hadad as a king who projected military power beyond Edom's borders. This is the same Midian that will later trouble Israel (the Midianite oppression of Judg. 6–8, ended by Gideon). Samlah of Masrekah — the sixth king — continues the non-dynastic succession: no father's name, a different city. The list of cities (Dinhabah, Bozrah, Avith, Masrekah) maps the geography of early Edom through its royal capitals. Waltke notes that the detail of Hadad's military campaign against Midian in Moab is the king-list's most historically specific data point, preserving a memory of early Edomite military activity in the region between Edom, Moab, and Midian.

verseByVerse.quote: Samlah died, and Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates reigned in his place. Shaul died, and Baal-hanan the son of Achbor reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary: Shaul of Rehoboth on the Euphrates is a striking geographical notation: a king of Edom who came from a city on the Euphrates — far north of Edom's traditional territory in Seir. The notation may indicate commercial or political connections between Edom and the upper Euphrates region, or it may identify a city named Rehoboth that existed in the Edomite context. The name Shaul (Saul) will also be the name of Israel's first king — the genealogies of both nations preserve this name independently. Baal-hanan son of Achbor — the eighth king — is the only Edomite king whose father's name is given, making him the closest to a dynastic succession in the list. Kidner notes that the appearance of a north Euphrates city in the Edomite king-list is one of the genealogy's most surprising geographical details, suggesting that early Edom's connections extended far beyond its Seir homeland.

verseByVerse.quote: Baal-hanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his place, the name of his city being Pau; his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab. These are the names of the chiefs of Esau, according to their clans and their localities, by their names: the chiefs Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
verseByVerse.commentary: Hadar — the eighth and last king in the list before the transition to the later Edomite chiefs — is the only Edomite king whose wife is named: Mehetabel, with her full maternal genealogy. The naming of the queen is unique in the king-list and may reflect the significance of Mehetabel's family in Edomite society. Then the transition to a second list of chiefs — different from the first list of vv.15–19, perhaps reflecting a later period of Edomite political organization. The first list of chiefs was organized by Esau's sons; this list (vv.40–43) is organized by clans and localities — a shift from genealogical to geographical organization that may reflect the political development of Edom over time. Wenham notes that the double chief-list reflects the genealogy's combination of different source materials, each providing a different organizational framework for the same population.

verseByVerse.quote: Oholibamah, Elah, Pinon, Kenaz, Teman, Mibzar,
verseByVerse.commentary: The second chief-list continues: Oholibamah (a chief with the same name as Esau's wife — either the same person elevated to chief status or a later namesake), Elah (a name that will appear in Israelite royal history), Pinon (a copper-mining site in Edom), Kenaz (an Edomite clan that will later assimilate into Judah — the Kenizzites of Gen. 15:19; Caleb the Kenizzite, Num. 32:12), Teman (the wisdom-associated region of southern Edom), and Mibzar. The appearance of Kenaz in the Edomite chief-list alongside the Kenizzites as a clan that will later be absorbed into Israel's tribal system illustrates the porousness of ethnic and national boundaries in the ancient world: an Edomite clan becomes a Judahite family. Waltke notes that the geographical and clan names in the second chief-list are more specific than the first list, suggesting later and more detailed political organization.

verseByVerse.quote: Magdiel, and Iram; these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau the father of Edom), according to their dwelling places in the land of their possession.
verseByVerse.commentary: The final two chiefs — Magdiel and Iram — complete the second list. The concluding summary — "these are the chiefs of Edom (that is, Esau the father of Edom)" — is the genealogy's final identification: Edom is Esau, and Esau is Edom. The parenthetical equation, appearing at both the beginning (v.1) and the end (v.43) of the chapter, frames the entire genealogy in the identity of the person: the nation is the man writ large. "According to their dwelling places in the land of their possession" — the geographical organization of the final summary affirms that Edom has a real land, real possessions, real territorial identity. The Esau who sold his birthright and despised his covenant inheritance has nonetheless produced a people with land and chiefs and kings. God's common-grace blessing operates even on the one who despised the covenant-grace blessing. Kidner writes that the closing equation of Esau and Edom is the chapter's theological summary: the man who chose the bowl of stew over the covenant promise became the father of a real and significant nation — and the genealogy honors that fact without endorsing the choice that produced it.

36.theology:
Genesis 36 teaches that God’s election of one people does not mean his contempt for others. Esau is not chosen for the covenant line; he is also not despised. His descendants fill Seir with chiefs, kings, and clans. God’s common grace extends to all nations, including those outside the covenant. Romans 9’s use of “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (from Malachi 1:2–3) is about covenant priority, not ontological rejection. Esau and his line live; they simply live outside the particular stream of redemptive history through which the Messiah will come.

The eight kings of Edom before Israel’s first king remind us that the world’s kingdoms develop according to their own logic while God’s kingdom advances according to a different logic—through barren women, younger sons, suffering servants, and a crucified King. The kingdom that looks most powerful by worldly metrics (Edom with kings) is not the kingdom through which God’s redemptive purposes run. The kingdom that looks weakest (a family of sojourners with no political standing) is the one that produces the Lion of Judah.
36.examples:
Genesis 36 is a pastoral reminder that God’s silence about someone in redemptive history is not God’s indifference to them. Esau gets a full genealogy; his descendants get named and honored. The pastoral implication is that those who feel they are outside the main story of what God is doing—not leaders, not gifted, not prominent in the life of the church—are not outside God’s care. Common grace is real grace. The God who numbers the hairs of his covenant people’s heads is also the God who notes that Anah found hot springs in the wilderness.

The non-dynastic kings of Edom—each dying without a son inheriting—illustrate the instability of human political orders not built on the foundation of God’s covenant. Human kingdoms come and go; the kingdom of God is unshakeable (Heb 12:28). The permanent king has yet to come when Esau’s kings are cycling through Edom. He will come from Judah—Leah’s son, the unloved wife’s son, by the sovereign grace that confounds every human calculation of worth.

37.title: Joseph's Dreams
37.text: Jacob lived in the land of his father’s sojournings, in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father’s wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father. Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors. But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him. Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. ... His brothers said to him, “Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?” So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words. ... They stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore. And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it. Then they sat down to eat. And looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry it down to Egypt. ... So when the Midianite traders passed by, they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty pieces of silver. They brought Joseph to Egypt. ... And they sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father and said, “This we have found; please identify whether it is your son’s robe or not.”
37.overview:
Genesis 37 opens the Joseph narrative, which will occupy the final fourteen chapters of Genesis and stands as the longest continuous narrative in the book. Joseph is one of the most sustained types of Christ in the entire Old Testament: the beloved son of his father, hated by his brothers without cause, stripped and sold for silver, descending into a pit, rising to the right hand of the ruler, and ultimately saving the very brothers who rejected him.

The chapter introduces the dynamics that will drive the entire story: Jacob’s favoritism (the robe of many colors), Joseph’s dreaming, the brothers’ murderous hatred, and the providential chain of events—pit, Ishmaelite traders, Egypt—that begins to fulfill what Joseph dreamed without either Joseph or his brothers understanding it.

Throughout the Joseph narrative, God is never directly mentioned as speaking or appearing. He works entirely through circumstances, human decisions, and the texture of ordinary life. Yet the theology of divine providence is more concentrated here than anywhere else in Genesis. “You meant it for evil; God meant it for good” (50:20) is the interpretive key that retrospectively illuminates everything in chapters 37–50. Providence works in the dark.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Genesis 37 opens the Joseph narrative — the longest continuous narrative in Genesis, spanning chapters 37–50. Joseph, the eleventh son of Jacob and the firstborn of Rachel, is his father's favorite: he receives the famous coat (or robe of distinction), he brings bad reports about his brothers to his father, and he has two dreams in which his brothers and parents bow down to him. The brothers' hatred culminates in a plot to kill him; Reuben diverts the plan to throwing him in a pit; the brothers sell him to Ishmaelite traders; the traders sell him in Egypt; and the brothers present the coat dipped in goat's blood to Jacob, who grieves inconsolably.
verseByVerse.theology: The Joseph narrative is structured around the dreams and their fulfillment: two dreams at the beginning (ch.37) and two pairs of dreams in the middle (chs.40-41) that will ultimately bring about the fulfillment of the original dreams in the reunion of chapters 42-45. The theological theme is divine providence operating through human wickedness: the brothers sell Joseph into slavery; God uses the slavery to place Joseph in the position where he will save the covenant family. Joseph's story is the most extended illustration in Genesis of the principle that 'what you intended for evil, God intended for good' (50:20).
verseByVerse.examples: Keller on Genesis 37: Joseph is a type of Christ at multiple points in his narrative — the beloved son sent by the father, rejected by his brothers, sold for silver, counted as dead, raised to unexpected glory, and ultimately the source of life for those who rejected him. The typology is not invented by the New Testament but embedded in the narrative itself: the specific details (coat, pit, silver, death reported to father) accumulate into a pattern that the careful reader recognizes as pointing beyond Joseph to a greater beloved Son.

verseByVerse.quote: Jacob lived in the land of his father's sojournings, in the land of Canaan. These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was pasturing the flock with his brothers. He was a boy with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. And Joseph brought a bad report of them to their father.
verseByVerse.commentary: The toledoth of Jacob opens what is actually the story of Joseph: the covenant patriarch's story is told through his son, as Isaac's story was told partly through his sons. Joseph at seventeen is working with the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah — the servant-women's sons — a detail that suggests he has a closer relationship with the younger brothers than with the older sons of Leah. The bad report to his father is the first indication of Joseph's character complexity: he is a young man who tattles on his brothers, which will not endear him to them. Whether the report was accurate or exaggerated, the effect is to create distance between Joseph and his brothers and to place him in a position of privilege and informational access with his father. Waltke notes that the opening portrait of Joseph — seventeen years old, working with the servants' sons, reporting on his brothers — establishes the family dynamics that will drive the conflict: Joseph is positioned as the informer and favorite before his dreams add the dimension of prophesied superiority.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons, because he was the son of his old age. And he made him a robe of many colors. But when his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his brothers, they hated him and could not speak peacefully to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Israel loved Joseph more than any other of his sons" — the narrator states the favoritism plainly, without editorial apology. The reason — "the son of his old age" — is the same reason given for parental favoritism throughout Genesis (and in 44:20, Benjamin will also be called the son of his old age). Jacob has not learned from his own experience as the non-favored twin; he replicates the partiality that shaped his own household. The robe (ketonet passim — a long-sleeved robe, or a robe of many colors, or a decorated tunic) is the visible, material sign of favoritism: it marks Joseph as different, as special, as the one who does not do manual field labor. The brothers cannot speak peacefully to him: the silence of hatred is more destructive than the anger of confrontation. They carry their resentment inward rather than expressing and resolving it. Kidner notes that the brothers' inability to speak peacefully to Joseph — not even the greeting of shalom — is the portrait of a family in which the fractures of parental favoritism have destroyed the fraternal bond.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joseph had a dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. He said to them, "Hear this dream that I dreamed:
verseByVerse.commentary: Joseph has a dream — and then tells it to his brothers. The telling of the dream, with its obvious implication of their subordination to him, is an act of either naivety (he genuinely doesn't understand how it will be received) or pride (he wants them to know). The brothers' response — increased hatred — is the predictable consequence. Young Joseph has not yet learned what the dreamer will need to learn over thirteen years in slavery and prison: that God's purposes require patience and silence, not premature proclamation. The invitation — "hear this dream that I dreamed" — is Joseph's first recorded speech, and it is simultaneously a claim to attention and an assertion of significance. He is presenting himself as someone whose dreams matter, someone whose visions are worth hearing. Waltke notes that Joseph's eager sharing of his dreams with his brothers is the act of a young man who has not yet learned the difference between having a gift and knowing how to steward it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf." His brothers said to him, "Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us?" So they hated him even more for his dreams and for his words.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first dream: sheaves in a field, Joseph's sheaf standing upright, the brothers' sheaves bowing to it. The agricultural imagery is specific and practical — sheave-binding is harvest work, and the field is the brothers' working world. The brothers immediately interpret the dream correctly: "are you to reign over us?" They are not wrong about the meaning; they are furious about the implication. The dream's significance is understood before it is fulfilled. The brothers' question is simultaneously the dream's interpretation and their indictment of Joseph: they see what the dream means and they hate it. "For his dreams and for his words" — the double cause of hatred is important: the dreams themselves (which they correctly interpret) and the words (the telling of the dreams, the presumption of sharing them). Wenham notes that the brothers' correct interpretation of the first dream establishes the interpretive key for the entire Joseph narrative: the dreams are real prophecy, correctly understood by everyone who hears them — the only question is whether the characters will trust or resist the divine plan they reveal.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers and said, "Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me." But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and said to him, "What is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come and bow ourselves to the ground before you?"
verseByVerse.commentary: The second dream escalates the scope: not just brothers but sun and moon — father and mother — bowing down. Joseph tells this dream also, apparently learning nothing from the first dream's reception. Jacob's rebuke is significant: even the father who loves Joseph cannot accept the implication that he will bow before his son. "Shall I and your mother and your brothers indeed come and bow ourselves to the ground before you?" — Jacob's question is the same question the brothers asked about the first dream, now extended to include the parents. The specific mention of "your mother" is puzzling (Rachel is dead by this point, 35:19) and may refer to the step-mother Leah, or may be a traditional formula for the father-mother-children family unit. The rebuke from Jacob is the first check on Joseph's premature declaration. Waltke notes that Jacob's rebuke, while real, is undermined by the narrator's note that he "kept the saying in mind" (v.11) — suggesting that even in rebuking the dream, Jacob took it seriously.

verseByVerse.quote: And his brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the saying in mind. Now his brothers went to pasture their father's flock near Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary: The brothers' jealousy is distinguished from their hatred: jealousy is the response to a perceived threat to one's own position; hatred is the active emotional state that drives action. Both are present, layered on top of each other. Jacob "kept the saying in mind" — the same phrase used in Luke 2:19 of Mary keeping the saying about Jesus in her heart. The patriarch who rebuked the dream publicly pondered it privately: perhaps these dreams mean something; perhaps this son is more than his favoritism has made him. The brothers go to Shechem — the place of the massacre of chapter 34, where Jacob was afraid of the inhabitants (34:30). The detail of Shechem as the destination establishes the geography of the coming confrontation: the brothers are far from home, beyond easy reach of their father. Kidner notes that the combination of jealousy + distance is the setup for every dangerous action in the story: resentment needs opportunity to become violence, and the isolation of Shechem provides the opportunity.

verseByVerse.quote: And Israel said to Joseph, "Are not your brothers pasturing the flock at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them." And he said to him, "Here I am." He said to him, "Go now, see if it is well with your brothers and with the flock, and bring me word." So he sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jacob sends Joseph to his brothers — the move that will initiate the entire sequence of slavery, Egypt, and eventual salvation. "Here I am" — the covenant availability (22:1, 7, 11; 31:11) spoken by Joseph in response to his father's call. He is sent to check on the welfare (shalom) of brothers who cannot speak shalom to him. The mission is entirely ordinary: a father worried about his sons, sending his favorite to check on them and report back. Nothing in the commission suggests catastrophe; everything in the reader's knowledge of the family dynamics suggests danger. The Valley of Hebron to Shechem is a journey of about fifty miles — a significant distance that places Joseph far from any protection. Waltke notes that Joseph's "here I am" in response to his father's sending anticipates the great missional pattern of Scripture: the Father sends the Son to the brothers with a message of shalom; the brothers reject both the message and the messenger.

verseByVerse.quote: A man found him wandering in the fields. And the man asked him, "What are you seeking?" He said, "I am seeking my brothers. Tell me, please, where they are pasturing the flock."
verseByVerse.commentary: A man finds Joseph wandering in the fields near Shechem — the brothers have already moved on. The unnamed man who provides directions to Joseph is one of the minor providential details of the narrative: without this man's information, Joseph would never have found his brothers at Dothan. The man's existence and his knowledge are part of the divine orchestration of the entire sequence. "What are you seeking?" — the question echoes through Scripture (John 1:38: "What are you seeking?" Jesus's first words to his disciples; Matt. 2:13: Herod seeking the child to destroy him). Joseph is seeking his brothers; his brothers are about to seek to destroy him. The seeking motif runs through the entire chapter: Jacob seeks news of his sons; Joseph seeks his brothers; the brothers seek to get rid of Joseph. Wenham notes that the anonymous man's role is to move Joseph from Shechem to Dothan, where the brothers are — the providential detail that makes the meeting possible.

verseByVerse.quote: And the man said, "They have gone away, for I heard them say, 'Let us go to Dothan.'" So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan. They saw him from afar, and before he came near to them they conspired against him to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary: The directions lead Joseph to Dothan — a city in the Jezreel Valley, further north than Shechem. The brothers see him from a distance — the robe, visible from far away, identifying him unmistakably. "Before he came near to them" — the conspiracy is formed at a distance, before Joseph can speak or interact. The sight of the robe triggers the hatred that has been building since the dreams. The conspiracy to kill is immediate and total: "let us kill him." The specific phrase — "conspired against him to kill him" — is the language of political assassination applied to a family conflict. Brothers conspiring to kill a brother is the pattern of Cain and Abel (4:8) enacted again in the covenant family. Waltke notes that the sight of the robe from a distance triggering the conspiracy reveals what drives the brothers' violence: not Joseph himself but the symbol of his father's favor that he carries on his body.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to one another, "Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him, and we will see what will become of his dreams."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Here comes this dreamer" — the contemptuous title is the brothers' own interpretation of who Joseph is: not a brother, not a person, but a dreamer — someone whose pretensions need to be eliminated. The plan is specific: kill him, throw the body in a pit, cover with the story of a wild animal attack. "We will see what will become of his dreams" — the brothers intend their violence as a theological argument: if we kill the dreamer, the dreams cannot be fulfilled; we will disprove the divine claim embedded in the dreams. They are setting themselves against the divine purpose embedded in Joseph's dreams. This is the pattern of those who oppose God's purposes: they believe that eliminating the human vehicle will eliminate the divine plan. But God's plans are not contingent on the survival of any particular human vehicle — a truth the brothers will learn when God uses their own violence to advance exactly the purposes they sought to prevent. Kidner writes that the brothers' taunt about the dreams reveals that they understood the theological stakes: they are not just killing a brother but attempting to nullify a divine purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Reuben heard it, he rescued him out of their hands, saying, "Let us not take his life." And Reuben said to them, "Shed no blood; throw him into this pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him"—that he might rescue him out of their hand, to restore him to his father.
verseByVerse.commentary: Reuben intervenes — the firstborn, whose authority should be greatest and who is most responsible for the welfare of the family. His proposal — throw him in the pit but don't kill him — is presented as the alternative to murder. The narrator reveals Reuben's true intention: to rescue Joseph later and return him to Jacob. Reuben is the only brother who intends to save Joseph, but his method is indirect and ultimately fails: he is not present when the Ishmaelites arrive (v.29), and his rescue plan is overtaken by Judah's sales proposal. Reuben's later distress (v.29: "he tore his clothes... where shall I go?"') reveals the genuine grief of a man who intended good but failed to act decisively enough. Waltke notes that Reuben's first act in the Joseph narrative — protecting the brother from the brothers — anticipates his ongoing role as the one who accepts responsibility (42:22, 37) even when he lacks the authority to enforce it.

verseByVerse.quote: So when Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the robe of many colors that he wore. And they took him and threw him into a pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The brothers execute the modified plan: strip the robe, throw Joseph in the pit. The stripping of the robe is the symbolic center of the action: they are removing the visible sign of Jacob's favor, the garment that provoked their hatred, the object that distinguished Joseph from them. The robe will next be used as evidence of Joseph's supposed death (v.31–33). The pit — empty, waterless — is Joseph's first imprisonment: a hole in the ground, unable to escape, with his brothers above him. The detail that there is no water is important: Joseph will not die of thirst in the pit, but the waterless pit is a figure of death — in later biblical imagery, the pit (sheol) is the place of the dead, the place without life-sustaining water. Kidner notes that the pit episode is the first of three imprisonments in Joseph's story (the pit, Potiphar's house prison, the royal prison) — each a descent that is followed by a rise, each a prelude to a more significant elevation.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they sat down to eat. And looking up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, with their camels bearing gum, balm, and myrrh, on their way to carry it down to Egypt. Then Judah said to his brothers, "What profit is it if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?
verseByVerse.commentary: The brothers sit down to eat after throwing Joseph in the pit — an act of callous indifference that will haunt them in Egypt (42:21–22: "we saw the distress of his soul when he begged us and we did not listen"). Then providential timing: the Ishmaelites appear. Judah's intervention is the sales proposal that saves Joseph's life while delivering him into slavery: "what profit is it if we kill him?" The argument is commercial, not moral: not "we should not do evil" but "we get nothing from killing him." The commodification of Joseph — he is worth twenty pieces of silver to the traders — is the nadir of the brothers' moral descent. But the sale that is motivated by profit rather than mercy is the act that will ultimately save the entire family. Waltke notes that Judah's sales proposal is simultaneously the worst moment of the brothers' action (reducing their brother to a commodity) and the providential turning point of the narrative: the sale to Egypt rather than murder in the pit is what enables the entire subsequent story.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let not our hand be upon him, for he is our brother, our own flesh." And his brothers listened to him. Then Midianite traders passed by. And they drew Joseph up and lifted him out of the pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. They took Joseph to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: "He is our brother, our own flesh" — Judah's restraint from murder is grounded in the biological connection: he is our brother. The same argument that Adam made for Eve (2:23: "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh") is invoked by Judah as the reason not to shed blood. The twenty shekels of silver — the price of a male slave between five and twenty years old (Lev. 27:5) — is the precise market value of a young man. Matthew 26:15 will note that Jesus was sold for thirty pieces of silver, the price of an adult male slave: the Joseph typology extends to the exact economic transaction. "They took Joseph to Egypt" — the narrative's most world-altering sentence since the expulsion from Eden. Egypt, the land Abraham visited in crisis (ch.12), the land Jacob was forbidden to enter (26:2), is now the destination of the covenant heir's son. Wenham notes that the casual sentence "they took Joseph to Egypt" conceals the entire drama of divine providence that will unfold across the remaining thirteen chapters of Genesis.

verseByVerse.quote: When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not in the pit, he tore his clothes and returned to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Reuben, who had planned to return and rescue Joseph, comes back to the pit to find it empty. His grief is immediate and physical: torn clothes, the sign of extreme distress. "The boy is gone, and I, where shall I go?" — the question is the cry of a man who has failed at the one act of responsibility he attempted. He had intended to save his brother; he was absent when the traders came; Joseph has been sold; the rescue plan has failed. The question "where shall I go?" echoes through the family's guilt: where does a man go when he has failed to protect the most vulnerable member of his family? The question is also the firstborn's acknowledgment of accountability: he is the one responsible, and now he must face his father. Kidner notes that Reuben's grief at the empty pit is the only expression of genuine distress among the brothers at this point — and even his grief is partly focused on himself ("where shall I go?") rather than entirely on Joseph's fate.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they took Joseph's robe and slaughtered a goat and dipped the robe in the blood. And they sent the robe of many colors and brought it to their father and said, "This we have found; please identify whether it is your son's robe or not."
verseByVerse.commentary: The brothers execute the cover story: the robe dipped in goat's blood, sent to Jacob with the request for identification. The deception is elaborately constructed and deliberately cruel: they do not tell Jacob directly; they send the bloodied robe and let him identify it. "Please identify" — the Hebrew word (haker-na) is the same word Tamar will use to Judah in chapter 38 ("please identify whose these are"): a verbal echo that connects the two deception stories and frames Judah as both deceiver and deceived. The robe that was the sign of Jacob's love is now the instrument of the brothers' deception: the garment of favor becomes the evidence of supposed death. Waltke notes that the brothers' use of the robe to deceive Jacob exactly inverts Jacob's use of clothing to deceive Isaac (27:15–16): Jacob deceived his father with his brother's garment; now Jacob is deceived by his sons using his favorite son's garment. The generational pattern of deception through clothing is exact.

verseByVerse.quote: And he identified it and said, "It is my son's robe. A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces." Then Jacob tore his garments and put sackcloth on his loins and mourned for his son many days.
verseByVerse.commentary: "Jacob tore his garments" — the same gesture of grief Reuben used at the empty pit (v.29), now performed by the father. Isaac was deceived by touch and smell; Jacob is deceived by sight — the bloodied robe is sufficient evidence. "A fierce animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces" — Jacob's grief is amplified by his certainty. He does not suspect his sons; he accepts the robe as evidence of the worst. The mourning that follows — sackcloth, many days — is the grief of the most loved father for the most loved son.
